title: 72-hour emergency kit
summary: Start with at least three days of safe water, ready-to-eat food, essential medicines, lighting and communication supplies. Include one gallon of water per person per day as a starting point, and account for pets, heat, medical needs and accessibility.
text: Does three days mean help will arrive then? No. Treat it as an initial reserve target and develop a longer-outage fallback based on safe water, care, sanitation and a verified supply or relocation option. Must everything fit in one box? No. Some water, care items or medicines require separate suitable storage. Record their locations and keep an independently manageable go-bag for leaving. Define what the kit is meant to support A 72-hour kit is a starting reserve for an interruption, not a guarantee that help returns in three days. Decide whether yours is mainly a home supply, a transportable evacuation reserve, or a combination with separate bags. The same volume and weight will not work for every purpose. A large home water reserve should not be treated as something everyone can carry out on foot. Build around needs, then choose containers Needs Count people, pets, care requirements, climate, and the services likely to fail. Supplies Select usable water, meals, lighting, communication, hygiene, and individual essentials. Access Choose storage and carry arrangements that work for the least mobile person. Editorial planning aid. Actual hazards, access needs and current instructions control the decision. Use the three-day goal to get started, then extend the reserve where practical. Count only usable supplies: safe water, familiar meals, compatible charging equipment, and items whose instructions you understand. Empty containers, expired consumables, and a battery without the right cable do not complete a need. Count water and meals as quantities CDC’s basic storage target is at least one U.S. gallon per person per day for three days, with additional needs considered and a longer reserve where possible. For two people, that baseline is six gallons; for four, twelve. The reserve needs to cover actual household use and extra needs, not just a bottle assigned to each bag. A headlamp can free a caregiver’s hands; a separate radio can preserve phone charge; a small power bank may support communication. None of these is a substitute for a specific powered-medical-equipment plan. Lights: choose controls and battery arrangements the users can manage. Keep a working light accessible outside the main bin. Charging: match cables and connectors, test them, and check manufacturer limits for any device you intend to support. Information: keep paper contacts, a local map or route information, and essential instructions with the kit. First aid: use supplies you know how to use and seek appropriate training. Owning a kit does not provide clinical skills. Comfort and weather: include suitable clothing and bedding for your actual climate without burying essential care items. title: A trusted neighbourhood support plan
summary: Build a small support network with people you already trust: agree check-ins, practical tasks and boundaries before a crisis. Share verified information and safe assistance without advertising stockpiles or exposing vulnerable people’s locations. Do not organise untrained rescues or assume outside supplies will arrive.

title: Adult & child choking
summary: If someone cannot speak, breathe or cough effectively, call emergency services. For a responsive adult or child, give 5 back blows followed by 5 abdominal thrusts, repeating until the blockage clears or they become unresponsive. Use chest thrusts when pregnant or when you cannot encircle the abdomen.

title: After a disaster: damage records, receipts and claims
summary: Protect people first. Once access is safe, document damage, keep receipts and contact your insurer through a verified channel. Do not enter an unsafe building to collect evidence.
text: Should I throw damaged items away immediately? Safety comes first. Where safe, document items before disposal and ask the insurer about inspection and evidence requirements. Do not retain hazardous materials in living areas merely to support a claim. A simple log is easier to maintain Editorial log columns: date; issue or item; photo filename; expense; person contacted; reference number; promised follow-up. Keep facts and estimates clearly separate. You do not need a polished report to preserve a useful chronology, but avoid overwriting the original evidence as your understanding changes. Separate urgent protection from permanent repair Write down which work is intended to prevent further damage and which work is a permanent repair. Ask the insurer what documentation is needed and keep relevant receipts. Do not sign unfamiliar assignments, blank forms or rushed contracts simply because someone says the offer expires today. Create an empty incident log today and photograph a few ordinary rooms for your private household inventory. Insurance coverage, deadlines and local law differ. This guide is recordkeeping help, not legal advice or a promise that costs will be paid. If the insurer cannot be reached, continue keeping safe evidence and receipts. title: Ammunition: compatibility, storage and inspection
summary: Use only ammunition confirmed for the exact firearm by its markings and manufacturer’s manual. Keep ammunition locked, dry, identifiable and away from unauthorized people; isolate uncertain or damaged rounds from use.
text: Is buying equipment enough? No. Check that it fits the intended task, can be used by the people who need it, and has a maintenance plan. Practice in safe conditions before relying on it. A simple inventory Record caliber exactly as labeled, manufacturer, lot when available, quantity and storage location in a private record. Inventory supports compatibility and accountability; it should not be posted publicly or attached to an easily shared household contact card. Review condition when checking storage, without unnecessarily manipulating cartridges. After flooding or household disruption Keep suspect ammunition separate from normal stock and restrict access. Do not try to restore wet ammunition by heating it. Disposal services and transport requirements differ; describe what you have and ask for instructions before taking suspect material to a facility. Audit labels and storage access. Mark anything uncertain as not for use and arrange appropriate professional advice. This guide does not provide reloading, ammunition manufacture, modification or performance optimization instructions. If reliable identification or inspection is unavailable, do not use the ammunition. Securing it and postponing use is safer than guessing from an online comparison photo. Keep keys, packaging and loose cartridges away from children and visitors. Include ammunition security in household relocation planning without giving untrained people responsibility for handling it. Ammunition ammo cartridges Keep labels intact Retain original packaging and identifying information. Do not mix loose cartridges or identify ammunition by appearance alone. Confirm compatibility Match the manual, firearm markings and ammunition packaging. Similar names or dimensions do not establish that a cartridge is safe for a firearm. Ask the manufacturer or a qualified professional if uncertain. Protect storage Use secured storage separate from unloaded firearms. Follow manufacturer guidance on moisture, heat and storage; keep oils, solvents and water away from ammunition. Stop using damaged or uncertain ammunition Do not fire corroded, deformed, flooded, contaminated or unidentified ammunition. Arrange lawful disposal through qualified local channels; do not burn, dismantle or throw it into a fire.

title: Apartment & high-rise fire
summary: If fire is in your apartment, leave by a safe route and close doors behind you. Use stairs, not elevators. If smoke or heat blocks the exit, keep the door closed, call the local emergency number and give your exact building, floor and apartment location.
text: A stairwell fills with smoke Do not continue into worsening smoke. Seek a protected location and tell responders exactly where you are. title: Armed conflict
summary: If fighting or explosions are nearby, move away from windows and exposed areas into the most protective intact space you can reach safely. Keep family members together, shoes and essential medicines close, and a plan for losing phone service. Do not cross active fighting for supplies or touch suspicious debris. Assistance and safe passage may be unavailable; judge movement against the danger of staying.

Conflict Choose shelter before the next attack Prefer a designated protective shelter if safely reachable. Otherwise use the most protective intact interior area available, away from glazing. Consider collapse, fire and flooding as well as blast exposure; no ordinary room guarantees safety. Keep essentials beside you Gather a battery light, footwear, safe water, medicines and written contacts without exposing yourself to retrieve them. Keep corridors and exits clear. Make a family check-in plan Choose nearby and out-of-area reunion contacts. Use short private messages with your location and status; do not publish live movements or other people’s locations. Reassess before moving Confirm a destination and route as recently as possible with independent trusted information. A claimed corridor or ceasefire is not proof of safe passage. Do not cross active fighting. Avoid explosive debris Leave unfamiliar objects, wires, fragments and abandoned munitions untouched. Warn people from a safe position and use verified demining or humanitarian channels when safe.

title: Avalanche
summary: Stay out of avalanche terrain when conditions are unsafe. Read the local avalanche forecast before travel and choose a safer route; rescue equipment does not make a dangerous slope safe. If someone is buried, call rescue and start companion rescue only where you can avoid another avalanche.
text: What matters before collecting supplies? Stay out of avalanche terrain when conditions are unsafe. Read the local avalanche forecast before travel and choose a safer route; rescue equipment does not make a dangerous slope safe. If someone is buried, call rescue and start companion rescue only where you can avoid another avalanche. Collect items only if doing so does not delay this action. What should another household member do? Use a second person to handle communication or dependents while the first carries out the immediate action. For avalanche, keep the specific hazard in view: Do not enter unstable terrain for an untrained rescue that may create more victims. What should be written down? Record when the situation changed, what action was taken and what remains uncertain. For this situation, start with: If an avalanche occurs. Note the last seen location, call rescue and assess continuing danger before searching. Keep personal notes private; they are not submitted to Osprey Zero.  Take a practical avalanche course and travel with trained partners. Use professional local advice for route selection. Do not enter unstable terrain for an untrained rescue that may create more victims. Without a working phone, prevention and trained companion rescue are even more important. Stay on terrain you have assessed as safe; do not enter a dangerous slope to find reception. Carry a written route and turnaround time with a trusted contact. Account for children, older people, pets and anyone who needs assistance before moving. Keep shoes, medicines and a torch in the shelter area. Decide who helps whom and who carries the essential supplies; do not send a lone child to retrieve items. For this situation, brief every person on the first action: check conditions before departure. Agree who will manage children, pets or mobility needs while that action happens. Do not enter unstable terrain for an untrained rescue that may create more victims. Mountain Check conditions before departure Consult the local avalanche center and get training before entering snow-covered backcountry. Choose terrain deliberately Avoid avalanche paths and slopes identified in the forecast; turn around when uncertain. Carry and know rescue gear Each person needs a transceiver, probe and shovel and practiced companion rescue skills. If an avalanche occurs Note the last seen location, call rescue and assess continuing danger before searching.

title: Baofeng basics: choose the radio, then learn its limits
summary: Baofeng is a brand, not permission to transmit. Identify the exact model, service certification, operator requirements and manual before programming or pressing transmit.
text: Is buying equipment enough? No. Check that it fits the intended task, can be used by the people who need it, and has a maintenance plan. Practice in safe conditions before relying on it. U.S. service distinctions FRS uses certified FRS equipment. GMRS requires appropriate certified equipment and applicable licensing. A generic programmable amateur handheld does not become a certified FRS or GMRS radio by entering those frequencies. Amateur radio has its own operator and station requirements; learn them through current official guidance and qualified local instruction. Rules outside the U.S. differ. Receiving alerts has limits A handheld that receives a weather broadcast may not provide reliable automatic alerts or SAME location-specific functions. Check the exact manual. Keep phone alerts and an appropriate weather radio as separate options. A charged radio is useful only when you know what to monitor and whether the desired service is available at your location. Find your exact manual and certification information, then write down the service, authorized users and a lawful routine test plan. Do not transmit on public-safety, aviation or other unauthorized channels. This is an equipment and planning overview, not legal authorization or programming instructions for a specific model. Use verified receive-only functions and your written contact plan while working out licensing or equipment questions. Do not assume that a crisis creates unrestricted permission to transmit on any frequency. Label the agreed channels and controls in plain language. Choose a radio that less technical household members can operate, not only one that an enthusiast can program. Two-way radios baofeng UV-5R ham radio Identify the exact radio Record model, regulatory identification and manual edition. Similar-looking radios can be intended for different services and markets. Separate receiving from transmitting A frequency you can enter is not automatically one you may transmit on. Check the relevant national radio service rules, licensing and device certification. Learn safe controls Use the exact manual to learn power, volume, channel selection, keypad lock and receive settings. Avoid transmit testing until you have confirmed permission and a suitable frequency or channel. Make a practical communication plan Choose compatible, lawful equipment with the people you need to reach. Test it in normal conditions at the locations you will actually use.

title: Battery backup: match the power source to the job
summary: List the devices you must support, check compatibility and test the real load before relying on a battery. Protect exits and follow the manufacturer’s charging and storage instructions.
text: The battery does not support the device? Use a compatible alternative; do not defeat safety limits or improvise adapters. Recharging depends on one unavailable source? Reduce the load and use the independent light and communications backup. Can I connect a portable battery to a wall outlet to power my house? Do not improvise a backfeed connection. Whole-home integration requires suitable equipment and qualified installation. Use only the connections and loads permitted by the actual product instructions. Make a device table before shopping Editorial table fields: device, required connection, normal use, intended backup period, compatible cable and tested result. Include the accessories; a charged power bank with the wrong cable cannot keep a phone working. For a refrigerator or other cycling appliance, a brief power reading alone does not establish whole-day runtime. Plan how the battery gets recharged Name an actual accessible charging source and the conditions that could prevent using it. Solar input depends on equipment compatibility and available conditions, so treat it as variable until tested. Keep a smaller independent light and communications option to avoid a single battery becoming the failure point for everything. Run one realistic test Editorial test: fully charge the suitable device, connect the actual appliance and cable, and record how long it serves the intended job under safe normal conditions. Repeat with the planned settings. Keep the result alongside the manual; do not extrapolate a brief test into a promise of overnight medical support. List three priority devices and verify their required connections. Test one planned charging session and record the result. Smoke, unusual heat, bulging, odors or noises can signal battery trouble. If a battery fire occurs, evacuate and call emergency services when reachable; do not attempt improvised firefighting or handle a failing battery. Check recalls. If charging is unavailable, reduce optional loads and reserve remaining power for agreed essentials. Seek another safe setting early if a critical device cannot be supported for the needed period. Teach the household which sockets and cables to use and who can change the setup. Keep batteries away from children and choose arrangements people can access without blocking doors. power bank portable power station battery backup Choose priorities Separate essentials such as communications and suitable lighting from optional loads. Medical equipment needs a supplier-approved backup plan, not a generic consumer battery assumption. Read the specifications Check output type, voltage, continuous output limits and device requirements. Capacity and maximum output answer different questions; a large capacity does not make every appliance compatible. Test in calm conditions Try the intended devices and cables within manufacturer limits. Record actual observed use and remaining capacity; do not plan around an untested marketing runtime. Make a safe charging routine Use appropriate charging equipment and follow product instructions. Inspect batteries for damage and keep charging arrangements clear of escape routes.

title: Boil-water advisory
summary: Use bottled water or bring clear tap water to a rolling boil for 1 minute, then cool it; above 6,500 feet, boil for 3 minutes. Use approved water for drinking, cooking and brushing teeth. Follow the exact local notice. Boiling does not remove chemical contamination.
text: Does my filter remove the need to boil? Do not assume it does. Household filters may not remove all germs, and some do not address the contaminant involved. Follow the actual advisory and the linked CDC instructions; use bottled water when boiling cannot be done safely. How do I avoid recontamination? Cool treated water safely and store in a clean, covered food-grade container. Keep dirty utensils and untreated water away from it. Mark the container and use a clean method to pour or dispense.  Keep bottled water and a safe means of boiling available. If boiling is impractical, use the alternative named by officials. A household pitcher filter does not replace boiling during this advisory. If fuel or electricity is unavailable, use sealed drinking water first. A treatment tablet is an option only for microbial risk and only when its label covers the conditions. If you cannot establish whether chemicals are involved, change the water source rather than experimenting. Keep one clearly marked clean-water supply for drinking, brushing teeth, food and medicine. Ask the care team about medical devices requiring special water. Powdered formula is not sterile; feeding plans need extra care for young or vulnerable infants. Water Confirm the notice Check that it is a boil-water advisory, rather than do-not-drink or do-not-use. Boil and cool Use the local authority instructions; allow water to cool safely before use. Prevent accidental use Avoid connected refrigerator water and ice; use safe water for food, formula and pets. Follow the all-clear Resume normal use only after official clearance and any flushing instructions.

title: Bug in: staying home with clear exit limits
summary: Staying home can be practical while the building is safe and essential needs can be met. Set explicit limits for leaving; stored supplies do not make fire, rising water, structural damage or severe exposure safe.
text: Does a large pantry mean I can stay indefinitely? No. The shortest essential limit may be care, water, sanitation, temperature or building suitability. Review each separately and keep a usable relocation option. Is staying home the same as sealing a room? No. Temporary sealing is a hazard-specific action, such as certain outdoor chemical instructions. A normal home-base utility plan does not automatically require it. Define staying home as a conditional decision “Bug in” means using home as the base during a disruption. It is sensible only while the dwelling is suitable and essential needs can be maintained. Supplies do not make a burning building, an evacuation zone, or failing essential care safe. Write the conditions for staying and the conditions that change the plan. A repeated stay-or-move decision Building Is the dwelling appropriate for the actual hazard and free from immediate internal danger? People Can care, safe temperature, water, food, and sanitation continue? Options Is a suitable relocation option reachable before the first essential need fails? Editorial decision framework. Do not remain against a hazard-specific evacuation instruction or in immediate danger. Separate a general home-base plan from hazard-specific shelter instructions. Staying home through a power interruption does not automatically require room sealing, and remaining in a tornado-threatened mobile home is not a protective shelter choice. Use the correct hazard guide alongside this household planning page. Check home suitability before buying more supplies List the location’s hazards and vulnerabilities: flood exposure, building condition, exits, heat or cold, shared systems, water supply, and care access. Ask what the home can actually provide when electricity and normal services fail. A full pantry does not compensate for an inaccessible exit or a medical device without a viable backup. Conditions for a workable home base Need Evidence to check Fallback Building protection Hazard-specific suitability and usable exits A different suitable shelter or evacuation destination. Essential care Individual care and equipment plan Provider-approved backup or another care setting. Temperature Actual indoor conditions and vulnerable people A confirmed safer heated or cooled location. Water and sanitation Safe supply and a functioning or contained hygiene arrangement Verified resupply or a suitable alternative location. Food and communication Usable meals and an accessible information channel Modest reserves and a checked contact arrangement. Do not assume ownership or familiarity proves suitability. A rental apartment, trailer, detached home, and rural property have different constraints. Write unresolved questions and investigate the ones that could stop essential care or safe movement first. Build a household base and a daily routine Choose an accessible area for the notebook, contacts, lights, and charging items. Keep exits and routes to the toilet clear. Put meal supplies and safe drinking water where they can be used without repeatedly unpacking the entire reserve. Keep waste, chemicals, and fuel separate from living and food areas. At the start of the day, check people, safe water, meals, care supplies, sanitation, and current information. During suitable daylight, handle necessary organization and safe resupply without leaving dependent people unsupported. Before dark, position lights, clear clutter, and arrange night care and the next check-in. Record what was used and any change that affects the stay-or-move decision. Give recurring tasks an owner and an alternate where possible; do not build the plan around one exhausted caregiver. A person living alone can use the same routine with an agreed outside check-in. Keep the plan workable if that contact fails, rather than making every daily task depend on a response. Choose meals and tasks that fit the available time, physical ability, and equipment. Long-duration blackout routine Hygiene with limited water Use supplies as a runway, not a reason to delay Count usable quantities and actual consumption. A tank or shelf capacity is not the amount present. Safe water, suitable meals, compatible backup energy, and available care consumables need separate counts. Do not merge them into a single preparedness score that hides the shortest essential supply. Example: a household has many days of pantry food but only a short supply of suitable drinking water and no confirmed resupply. Its staying decision is driven by the water problem, not the food total. Similarly, provider-directed care limits can be more urgent than any ordinary supply calculation. A simple home status log Record Use it to decide Amount and condition Count what is actually safe and functional. Measured daily use Estimate when resupply or a move becomes necessary. Confirmed next source Identify whether it can be reached and what it provides. Transport and destination Preserve an option to leave before it is lost. Uncertainty Mark assumptions rather than recording guesses as facts. Use conservative planning allowances for uncertainty without restricting necessary drinking water or prescribed care. Review after guests arrive, weather changes, a container leaks, or an important device fails. A notebook should show the change and the next action, not only the original target quantities. Set exit triggers and a ready departure plan Decide the conditions that require leaving, who notices them, and what action follows. Immediate hazards need immediate protective action. Developing shortages allow an earlier planned relocation while transport and a suitable destination are still available. Avoid waiting until a need has already failed to ask whether another location is open. An applicable evacuation instruction changes the home-base plan; use current hazard and route guidance. A fire, CO alarm, unsafe flood exposure, or failing building requires the relevant immediate response. Loss of essential care uses the person-specific urgent-care or backup plan. Inability to maintain suitable water, sanitation, or temperature requires verified alternatives and a realistic relocation decision. Keep manageable bags and daily-use grab lists ready so a change of plan does not start with a full-house search. Confirm the destination’s access, care, and pet arrangements. Keep an alternate and the outside contact informed when safe. Securing possessions is secondary to leaving danger. A decision to stay this morning should not become a commitment to stay regardless of what happens later. Run a tabletop drill and review recovery Use an editorial exercise with three stages. First, normal electricity fails. Second, the expected restoration moves back a day. Third, the planned water source is closed. Ask the household what changes at each stage, who acts, and what information is still missing. Keep real care and utilities operating during the exercise. Find the current supply and contact record. Identify the shortest essential limit and the matching action. Check who supports dependents while someone gathers information or supplies. Explain the destination and transport alternative if home becomes unsuitable. Record the first three practical gaps and choose one affordable improvement. After a real disruption, check recovery by system: electricity, water, drainage, food storage, and access. Service returning in one does not clear every other hazard. Replenish used reserves, revise unrealistic assumptions, and review the plan with the people who use it. A simpler maintainable plan often provides more value than another box of unused equipment. Test a two-hour no-mains-power routine in safe conditions, keeping essential medical equipment and food safety protected. Bugging in is not barricading yourself into a hazardous building. Keep fire exits usable and follow the protective action appropriate to the threat. Use a written routine and reachable support contacts. Conserve existing essentials by reducing unnecessary use, while meeting actual drinking, hygiene and care needs. If the home becomes unsafe, supplies must not be a reason to stay. Plan for a person who needs powered equipment, temperature-controlled medicine, assistance on stairs or sensory support. Identify a helper and alternative location rather than assuming the building manager can provide one. Bug out & bug in bug in bugin stay home Define staying home as a conditional decision Check home suitability before buying more supplies Build a household base and a daily routine Use supplies as a runway, not a reason to delay Set exit triggers and a ready departure plan Run a tabletop drill and review recovery Assess the building and hazard Check fire, gas, carbon monoxide, flooding, structural damage, indoor temperature and the current warning. A general stay-home plan differs from a chemical shelter-in-place instruction. Map essential needs Plan drinking water, safe food, hygiene, light, communication, medications, cooling or warmth, and support for dependents. Count people and pets before estimating supply duration. Set review points Choose who checks conditions, supplies and messages at agreed times. Log important changes and avoid constant battery-draining news consumption. Keep an exit ready Keep medicines, documents, shoes, mobility aids and bags accessible. Write the conditions that would require a safer destination and how you would get there.

title: Bug out: evacuation destinations, triggers and routes
summary: A useful bug-out plan names when to leave, where to go, how to travel and what to do if the first option fails. The destination matters more than an overloaded bag.
text: Is a distant rural location a sufficient destination? No. Verify access, acceptance, shelter, safe water, sanitation and essential care. An unfamiliar location can introduce needs the household is not equipped to meet. How many routes should I have? Develop realistic alternatives where possible and check current conditions. Several lines on a map are not helpful if they share the same closure or cannot be used by the household. Build an evacuation plan with a real destination “Bug out” is planned relocation from an unsafe place. Define it in ordinary terms: who leaves, under what conditions, by what transport, to which suitable destination. A vague plan to head into the countryside creates new problems with shelter, water, access, and permission. Choose locations that can actually support the household. A complete relocation chain Trigger A recognizable hazard instruction or household condition starts the departure plan. Journey Suitable transport and current route information support the whole household. Arrival A checked destination meets access, care, pet, and sleeping needs. Alternative Another realistic option handles a closed route, unavailable driver, or rejected arrival. Editorial planning aid. Actual hazards, access needs and current instructions control the decision. Keep immediate escape distinct from planned evacuation. If the building is burning or another immediate danger is present, leave without finishing a bag or route worksheet. For a developing hazard, the planning chain helps the household move before choices become limited. Choose triggers you can recognize Write conditions rather than dramatic predictions. Examples include an applicable evacuation instruction, an unsafe dwelling, or the inability to continue essential care. Some care or transport needs require an earlier departure than a general deadline. Use individual provider and equipment guidance instead of inventing a generic timing rule. Turn a concern into a decision Concern Trigger to define Action to prepare Regional hazard Applicable zone or address instruction and relevant deadline Use the current route and suitable destination. Building suitability Immediate danger or verified loss of safe use Use the appropriate escape and accommodation plan. Essential care Individual backup or care limit Move or seek urgent assistance according to the care plan. Transport A point beyond which the option becomes unavailable Arrange an earlier usable departure. Safe water or sanitation Cannot sustain the need with verified alternatives Relocate before supplies or containment fail. For an outdoor chemical or radiation emergency, travel can increase exposure. A relocation plan should include the possibility of sheltering under the specific instruction, rather than treating departure as always correct. Keep the hazard-specific guidance available with the trigger sheet. Develop two destinations and check their assumptions Choose a primary and an alternate location, considering the hazards likely to affect both. Two addresses on the same exposed street may share the same failure. Options can include a consenting trusted contact, suitable accommodation, or an operating designated shelter, but acceptance and services need checking. Record the address, contact, acceptance arrangement, and how to reach it without an internet search. Check access, essential equipment support, medicine storage, sleeping, water, sanitation, and any specific dietary needs. Confirm pet rules and a suitable transport arrangement for the animals actually owned. Identify what each location expects the household to bring. Record when the information was checked and the alternative if the destination is unavailable. Example: family offers a spare room, but the only toilet is upstairs and a household member cannot use stairs. The address is willing but not suitable without a workable accommodation. Resolve that detail before calling it the primary destination. Do not turn a friendly offer into a promise of medical or specialist support. Connect routes, vehicles, and carrying capacity Choose more than one route where practical, but regard them as options to check against current conditions. A paper map or saved route note supports orientation; it does not certify that a road is open. Follow applicable closures and hazard-specific instructions and do not drive through flooded or actively dangerous routes. Test the complete transport load Part What to verify People Seats, driver, pickup location, and access assistance. Care equipment Usable space and the appropriate support during travel. Pets Secure transport and suitable carriers or restraints. Bags Manageable loading without displacing people or essential equipment. Fuel or charge Available reserve and realistic stops; do not assume every service remains open. No-vehicle fallback A confirmed helper or assistance option, with limits and an alternate. Walking is not simply the same plan without a car. Reassess distance, conditions, mobility, water, carrying capacity, and route safety. Arrange support early where possible. Do not use a prolonged survival march as the default answer to an unavailable vehicle. Evacuation without a car Go-bag packing Prepare roles, bags, and change messages Name who supports each dependent person, who handles pets, who manages transport, and who communicates. Include an alternate for an adult who may be away. Keep individual bags and a short list of daily-use care items ready, and test that the helpers can carry what they are assigned. For a planned departure, confirm people and urgent care requirements first. Check the destination and current route. Collect manageable bags and daily-use items if time permits. Tell the outside contact the destination, people present, and next check-in when safe. At arrival, count everyone and settle essential care. If the plan changes, send one concise updated destination message instead of relying on several different assumptions. Protect privacy when sharing information. Trusted contacts may need the route and care requirements; a public social-media audience generally does not need the household’s exact departure, documents, or empty-home details. Communication should support safety and reunion, not create another task that delays leaving. Keep the immediate-escape rule visible on the role sheet: no optional item is worth remaining in or re-entering danger. A beautifully packed bag should reduce departure effort, not become a reason to postpone it. Rehearse one failed assumption at a time Start with a tabletop walk-through, then safe practical checks such as loading the proposed equipment or walking the normal building exit route. Do not practise a hazardous journey, shut down essential medical equipment, or enter restricted areas. Use discussion to introduce a road closure, unavailable driver, or closed destination. Ask another adult to explain the trigger and find the destination information. Check how children, pets, and equipment fit into the departure sequence. Time ordinary retrieval only to identify a missing item or awkward arrangement, not to encourage unsafe rushing. Write what changes if the primary route or location fails. Review when household needs, vehicles, destinations, or local arrangements change. After a real move, record what was actually useful and what caused delay. Replenish the bag, update the acceptance arrangements, and revise unrealistic alternatives. Plan the return separately using current access and building-safety information. The goal is a usable relocation system that can change with conditions, not an unalterable route drawn on a map. Immediate evacuation actions Household emergency plan Time a calm departure rehearsal with the actual people, bags and transport. Record the slowest step and fix it. No universal bug-out destination or timetable suits every disaster. Avoid flooded roads and do not enter an active danger area for supplies. Work from confirmed reachable options and supplies already accessible. Help may be delayed, so keep your own contacts, route notes and essential care information available without internet. Assign an adult to each dependent and identify who can drive or arrange accessible transport. Check shelter rules for pets, service animals and support equipment before an event. Bug out & bug in bug out bugout Build an evacuation plan with a real destination Choose triggers you can recognize Develop two destinations and check their assumptions Connect routes, vehicles, and carrying capacity Prepare roles, bags, and change messages Rehearse one failed assumption at a time Choose departure triggers Write hazard-specific triggers: evacuation instructions, unsafe building conditions, approaching wildfire, flood access loss or inability to sustain essential care. Leave before routes become unsafe where possible. Confirm destinations Arrange a nearby and an outside-area destination. Check acceptance, accessibility, pets, parking and essential care. An unconfirmed shelter or public campground is not a guaranteed destination. Plan transport and alternatives Map at least two practical routes where available. Consider no-car travel, fuel, road closures, bridges, water hazards and travel time with dependents. Make a short grab list Prioritize medicines, identification, contacts, mobility aids, keys, phone power, water and weather protection. Assign bags and dependent care; never delay an urgent departure to complete packing.

title: Burns & scalds
summary: Stop contact with the heat source safely. Cool a thermal burn promptly with clean running water for 5-20 minutes while preventing whole-body chilling, then loosely cover it with a clean nonadherent dressing. Seek urgent help for deep, large, sensitive-area burns or breathing trouble.
text: No running water Use clean available water and seek clinical guidance; do not use floodwater or contaminated water. Avoid improvised creams while awaiting assessment. Smoke inhalation Breathing trouble, facial burns or soot around nose or mouth needs urgent medical help, even if the skin burn seems limited. Should I wrap it tightly? No. Use a loose clean nonadherent covering after cooling; swelling can make a tight wrap dangerous.  Seek professional assessment for serious burns and worsening pain, redness or fever. Chemical and electrical injuries need their own assessment even when skin damage looks small. Do not apply ice directly, butter or toothpaste. Do not break blisters. This cooling sequence is for thermal burns, not every chemical exposure. Use clean available water to cool the thermal burn while seeking assessment; keep the unburned body warm. Breathing difficulty or smoke around the mouth or nose requires urgent help. Do not turn lack of specialist access into a reason to apply household remedies. A child can cool too quickly during whole-body showers. One caregiver should watch temperature and breathing while another manages water and contact with care. Keep labels or exposure details when chemicals or electricity were involved, without carrying contaminated items into a clean area.  Stop the exposure Move away from the heat safely. Do not touch an electrically injured person until the power source is safely isolated. Cool the burned area Use clean running water promptly for 5-20 minutes. Keep the rest of the person warm, especially children; stop whole-body chilling. Remove tight items Remove jewelry and tight items before swelling if they are not stuck. Do not pull away material adhering to the skin. Cover and seek assessment After cooling, loosely cover with a clean nonadherent dressing. Get prompt care for deep burns, burns larger than the person’s palm or those involving face, hands, feet or genitals.

title: Bushcraft: a practical beginner’s foundation
summary: Learn shelter, navigation, water planning and equipment care on short, supported trips. Bring reliable essentials first; practice should not depend on catching food, making fire or improvising every item.
text: Is buying equipment enough? No. Check that it fits the intended task, can be used by the people who need it, and has a maintenance plan. Practice in safe conditions before relying on it. Choose skills with immediate value A tarp pitched securely, dry clothing and a known route home usually offer more value than dramatic survival experiments. Test your equipment with the people who will use it. Record what failed: a cord too short, wet insulation, a leaking bottle, an unreachable headlamp or an overly heavy pack. Food, water and fire boundaries Bring food rather than relying on hunting or foraging. Clear water is not automatically safe. A filter must match the contamination hazard and its instructions; chemical contamination can require another source. Treat fire as optional: restrictions, wind, wet conditions and fuel availability may prevent safe use. Do not build a trip plan around a fire you may be unable or prohibited to light. Run a daylight shelter-and-packing session close to home. Finish with a gear check and a written lesson learned. No eating unidentified plants, unsafe knife experiments, destructive shelters or unsupervised fire practice. Outdoor skills require hands-on training and judgment. Use the equipment and safe route you brought. Turn back early if conditions exceed your ability, your group is tiring or essential equipment fails. If lost, stop and use the lost-outdoors plan rather than experimenting with shortcuts. Choose distance and terrain for the least mobile person. Include individual medicines, warm layers and snacks. Give every person a light, whistle and simple instructions for separation. Bushcraft bushcraft bushcrafting Choose a low-consequence practice site Use a permitted location near an easy return route. Check weather, land rules and water availability; tell someone your itinerary and return time. Pack dependable essentials Bring navigation, a headlamp, insulation, weather protection, water, food, first aid and a shelter appropriate to conditions. Tools complement these supplies. Practice one skill at a time Pitch a shelter, organize a dry sleeping system or locate yourself on a map before adding complications. Practice before dark with enough time to stop. Leave a clean site Use existing durable sites where permitted. Carry out waste and follow local rules for fires, wood collection and wildlife protection.

title: Carbon monoxide
summary: If a CO alarm sounds or carbon monoxide exposure is suspected, get everyone into fresh air immediately and call emergency services. Do not stay inside to find the source. Headache, dizziness, nausea or confusion can be warning signs.
text: Can I turn off the appliance first? Move everyone to fresh air before investigating. A fuel-burning appliance may continue exposing people while it is being inspected. Call from outside and do not reenter until the hazard has been assessed by appropriate qualified personnel. Can the household sleep elsewhere inside? Changing rooms is not a reliable answer to a suspected CO exposure. Get outside to fresh air and seek medical evaluation for symptoms. Keep people together so confusion, faintness or worsening breathing is noticed.  Install CO alarms and service heating equipment. Keep generators and grills outdoors, far from openings. CO is invisible and odorless. A silent smoke alarm is not proof that air is safe. Leave the building even if responders cannot be reached. Gather outside away from exhaust, keep everyone out and seek reachable medical care for symptoms. Do not send someone back inside to ventilate or switch equipment off. Children, sleeping people and people with limited mobility may not recognize symptoms or reach fresh air independently. Assign evacuation help in advance and keep functioning CO alarms near sleeping areas. Do not make a symptomatic person drive. Air & gas Leave the building Move people and pets into fresh air, without delaying to ventilate or troubleshoot. Call from outside Report the alarm, symptoms and possible fuel-burning source to emergency services. Get medical help Tell responders about suspected exposure even if symptoms improve outdoors. Wait for clearance Do not reenter until responders say it is safe.

title: Caregiver handover: a plan for missed visits
summary: Write down essential tasks, confirm who can perform them safely, and define when a missed visit becomes urgent. A name on a contact list is not a confirmed backup caregiver.
text: What if my usual helper also needs to evacuate? Agree a second helper or destination before the emergency. Ask both helpers about the conditions that would make them unavailable so the backups do not all fail together. Keep the summary short and current Editorial format: one page for the immediate routine, with detailed instructions and specialist plans stored separately. Date the summary and name who updates it. Have a backup helper explain the plan back to you; confusing wording discovered in a calm practice run is easier to fix than during an outage. Test the access problem A helper may know the routine but be unable to enter the building or reach supplies. Discuss keys, building rules and any safe access arrangement without publishing codes. Include what happens when lifts stop or transport is disrupted. Do not make the entire backup depend on a single phone, driver or person. Run a calm handover exercise with the backup helper. Record one task they cannot perform and arrange a qualified alternative. Generic emergency advice does not replace an individual clinical or equipment plan. Do not improvise lifting, feeding, medication changes or medical-device work. If no helper can attend, use the individual plan to prioritize safe independent tasks and seek reachable assistance early. A situation involving essential care that cannot be delivered may require moving to a setting that can support it. Include the person receiving care in decisions. Protect their privacy and ask about language, hearing, vision and communication needs. Ensure helpers know who can authorize changes to the plan. care handover missed caregiver support network List the next essential tasks Record what must happen during the next day: meals, personal care, medicines, equipment checks and mobility assistance. Separate everyday help from tasks requiring training. Confirm responsibility Ask a primary and backup helper what they can actually do, when they can arrive and what supplies or access they need. Do not assign clinical work to an untrained volunteer. Write a short handover Record the usual routine, communication preferences, relevant contacts, supply locations and limits. Share with consent through a private method. Set escalation points Agree what happens if the person cannot be reached, a critical task is missed or the environment no longer supports care. Identify a realistic accessible destination before that point.

title: Checkpoints & interrupted travel
summary: Avoid unnecessary travel through active fighting or uncertain checkpoints. title: Child & infant CPR
summary: If a child or infant is unresponsive and not breathing normally, call the local emergency number, begin CPR and get an AED. Compressions plus breaths are important for children and infants. Follow dispatcher coaching and current hands-on training.

If a container’s history is unclear or it may be contaminated, do not count it as confirmed drinking water. Plan meals and dispensing around the reserve Water use includes what meals require. Write a sample day of familiar food and note every step needing water: preparation, drinking, cleanup, and care. An emergency pantry full of foods that need long boiling can be a poor match for limited water and fuel. Include options that need little or no preparation water. Keep a clean dispensing method with the container. Avoid repeatedly dipping hands or a used cup into the supply. Agree which containers are for everyday use during the disruption and which remain closed as reserve. Allocate suitable water for pets and any provider-directed care requirement. Keep drinking-quality water available for brushing teeth and food preparation during a water advisory, as directed by that notice. Do a tabletop exercise: list tomorrow’s meals, estimate the water used, then compare it with a day of actual routine use. The exercise reveals omitted tasks without deliberately depriving anyone of water. Use the result to improve storage and reduce unnecessary water-heavy tasks. Storage is only one layer of the water plan A reserve buys time; it does not establish an unlimited source. Identify how you would obtain suitable water if the disruption exceeds your stock: a confirmed retailer, distribution point, trusted person, or other verified supply. Record access, carrying capacity, and the possibility that the location is closed. Do not count swimming-pool water, floodwater, an unknown stream, or chemically contaminated water as drinking supply. Boiling and ordinary filters do not solve every contamination problem. If tap service fails or an advisory is issued, use the water-outage guide to determine the allowed uses and the next safe source. Water outage and advisories Long-duration blackout planning Learn the local advisory system. Plan how to transport water if distribution sites open. Do not reuse containers that held toxic substances, even after washing. Calculate the household quantity on paper and store smaller containers if lifting a large container is difficult. Keep one portable supply ready. Divide storage between safe places so damage to one container does not lose all the household water. Choose container sizes and dispensing positions that the least mobile household member can use. Include pets, guests, hot-weather needs, pregnancy, illness, and provider-directed care needs in the quantity plan. Ask another capable person to locate and explain the reserve. Keep drinking and non-drinking containers clearly distinct. Water & food Work out the household quantity Choose containers you can actually handle Clean, fill, and label without confusion Store for access as well as capacity Make rotation a simple routine Plan meals and dispensing around the reserve Storage is only one layer of the water plan Calculate needs Count people and days and add water for pets and extra needs. Choose containers Use commercially bottled water or food-grade containers intended for water. Label and store Mark fill dates and store away from sunlight, fuel and cleaning products. Rotate supplies Follow bottled-water dates and replace self-filled stored water every six months.

title: Evacuating with pets
summary: Take pets when you can evacuate safely, using a carrier or lead and a destination that accepts them. Keep food, water, medicines, identification and veterinary information together. Do not delay escape into immediate danger or reenter a hazardous building for an animal.
text: Take pets when you can evacuate safely, using a carrier or lead and a destination that accepts them. Keep food, water, medicines, identification and veterinary information together. Do not delay escape into immediate danger or reenter a hazardous building for an animal.  Are pets accepted wherever people shelter? Do not assume so. Verify the particular site’s current admission, containment and care arrangements, including any separate housing. Keep an alternative suitable destination. What if a pet is still inside a dangerous building? Do not reenter active danger. Give reachable responders accurate information from safety and use verified animal-assistance channels when available. Make a separate departure task for every animal Name who collects each animal, which carrier or restraint is used, and where the animal will travel. Include pets that hide, cannot be handled by every adult, or need special care. Start containment early in a developing evacuation when it is safe; searching for a frightened cat after doors open can consume the departure time. Keep the human immediate-escape plan separate from planned packing. Plan the animal’s whole journey Contain Use suitable familiar restraint or a secure carrier before loading. Move Fit people, animals and essential care equipment into the actual transport. Receive Confirm an animal-compatible destination and care arrangement. Editorial planning aid. Actual hazards, individual needs and current instructions control the response. Editorial example: two dogs have bags of food ready but only one adult can safely handle both leads while helping a child. The gap is responsibility and transport, not food. Practice a calm loading sequence in normal conditions and adjust the plan before warning time is short. Do not delay escape from a fire or reenter danger to collect equipment or an animal. Confirm admission rather than assuming a shelter accepts pets Check the destination directly before relying on it. Ask whether it accepts the animal’s species, size and number, what containment and records are required, whether animals stay with owners, and what care remains the owner’s responsibility. A hotel, host, boarding facility or evacuation center may have different rules and limited space. Keep a realistic alternative that is not exposed to exactly the same hazard. A useful destination confirmation Question Record the actual answer Acceptance Species, number and any relevant restrictions. Admission Opening, availability, reservation or registration requirements. Equipment Carrier, lead, records, food and other supplies required. Care Who feeds, handles and gives prescribed medicines. Separation Where animals stay, visiting arrangements and how ownership is verified. Do not conflate pets and service animals. They may have different accommodation rules. Red Cross guidance describes possible separate animal housing depending on circumstances and welcomes service animals that assist people with disabilities. Use the specific facility’s current arrangements; do not present an old shelter list or general policy as a confirmed space for tonight. Pack usable care, identification and a concise instruction card Use the normal suitable food, safe water, appropriate bowls, prescribed medicines and needed waste supplies. Count pet water and food separately so human reserves are not silently assigned twice. Include the equipment needed to open or serve the actual food. Ask the veterinarian about special diets, medicine storage and emergency care needs; do not improvise a dose or sedate an animal from a generic evacuation tip. Keep a suitable carrier, harness or lead with an accessible loading location. Use a current identification tag and review microchip contact details where applicable. Keep a recent photograph and veterinary information privately with the responsible adult. Write the feeding routine, prescribed instructions, veterinarian contact and important handling needs. Include appropriate waste containment and clean-up supplies without packing chemicals beside food. Add a familiar item if manageable, while keeping essential human and animal care accessible. Label by animal where needs differ. A generic bag saying pets can conceal a missing medicine or the wrong food. Keep a grab list for daily-use care items and review it after treatment changes. Store records so they can be found even if a phone fails, while protecting information that is unnecessary for admission or care. Test transport space and controlled loading Check the actual vehicle with people, mobility equipment, bags and suitable animal restraint. Carrier dimensions and access matter as much as total cargo space. Use the restraint and transport equipment as intended and maintain appropriate ventilation and temperature. Never leave an animal in a hot vehicle while negotiating admission or checking a room. Travel conditions and the animal’s health may require veterinary advice. A calm loading rehearsal Check Problem it reveals Carrier access An animal cannot enter calmly or the door does not secure. Responsible handler The assigned adult is also needed for another dependent person. Vehicle layout People or essential equipment lose necessary space. Transfer at arrival Opening a door creates an escape opportunity. Backup driver The alternative vehicle cannot fit the same arrangement. Keep doors and animals controlled during transfers. Do not let children manage a distressed animal beyond their ability. If the usual adult is away, identify a trusted helper with appropriate access and knowledge before the emergency, rather than counting on an unfamiliar volunteer. A helper must also have a safe route; do not ask them to enter active fire, floodwater or another dangerous area. Maintain care in temporary accommodation On arrival, count animals and confirm that each is secured in the intended arrangement. Place food, medicines and clean equipment where the responsible person can find them. Keep animals under appropriate control around unfamiliar people and other animals. Distress can change behavior, so do not assume a normally friendly animal is comfortable with crowding, noise or strangers handling it. Keep a daily care record if responsibility changes Record feeding, prescribed care, waste needs and any concern for the next trusted handler. Note what was actually done rather than leaving two adults to guess whether medicine was already given. Check temperature, available water and suitable rest without relying only on the weather outdoors. Seek veterinary help for worrying changes or injury. Maintain hygiene between animal waste, meal tasks and child care. If separate boarding is necessary, verify who holds the animal, how updates are obtained, and how collection will work. Keep the information with the household coordinator so onward movement does not leave the animal unaccounted for. Plan lost-pet checks and safe return If an animal is missing, record its last confirmed place and time, description, identification and photograph. Contact verified animal services, veterinary contacts or the relevant facility through independently obtained channels when available. Do not enter a dangerous area or pay an unknown caller solely on a claim of finding the animal. Keep public appeals limited to useful information and protect private identity and location details. Account for each animal before every move and after arrival. Tell the trusted handler or household coordinator of any missing animal. Record sightings separately from confirmed identification. Verify found-animal reports through a known service or safe trusted contact. Confirm collection and update outdated notices when reunited. Return home only when the setting is suitable for people and animals. Keep animals controlled around damage and debris. After an evacuation, review the part that actually failed: capture, loading, admission, care or communication. Replace used supplies and adjust responsibility before the next event. Livestock, large numbers of animals and specialist species need their own transport and welfare plan; this household guide does not make a small pet carrier plan sufficient for them. Household evacuation Returning home Check animals regularly for overheating, cold and distress in transport. Keep them restrained in crowded temporary accommodation and maintain hygiene. A service animal and a pet may have different accommodation rules. Never leave animals in a hot vehicle while arranging shelter. Use a confirmed trusted host or animal-care arrangement and keep a viable alternative. Ask the actual evacuation site about current animal housing rather than assuming every site accepts pets or keeps them beside their owners. Assign a capable handler to each animal while another adult manages children or access needs. Test transport with the actual people and equipment, and verify pet and service-animal arrangements separately. pets evacuation dog evacuation cat emergency Make a separate departure task for every animal Confirm admission rather than assuming a shelter accepts pets Pack usable care, identification and a concise instruction card Test transport space and controlled loading Maintain care in temporary accommodation Plan lost-pet checks and safe return Contain animals early Use a secure carrier or lead before loading or opening doors. Distress and noise can cause animals to run. Confirm the destination Ask whether pets are accepted and what documents or carriers are needed. Make a backup arrangement with a trusted person. Pack basic care Take normal food, safe water, medicines, waste supplies and a familiar blanket if readily available. Include pet water in the household total. Keep identification current Use a tag and a recent photo, and check microchip contact details before emergencies. Keep veterinary records privately. Avoid unsafe rescue Tell reachable responders where an animal may be, but do not return to fire, floodwater or active danger yourself.

title: Evacuation
summary: Leave a threatened location while a safer route and destination are still available. Take people, pets, essential medicines, identification, shoes, water and phone power; do not delay for belongings. Confirm the route and a place to stay, tell a trusted contact, and avoid flooded, closed or actively dangerous roads. Do not wait for an order when immediate danger is evident. Radiation or airborne hazards may make sheltering safer than travel.
text: A departure is easier when the destination and route are already decided. Your first destination is closed? Use the checked alternate and tell the outside contact when safe. A vehicle is unavailable? Use the early transport arrangement; see evacuation without a car. Do not wait until travel conditions deteriorate to investigate capacity. Should I finish packing before escaping a fire? No. Leave immediate danger and do not return for belongings. A planned regional departure may allow a short preparation sequence; urgent escape does not. What if the destination changes? Use a suitable checked alternative and notify the outside contact when safe. At arrival, account for people and verify essential care rather than assuming the original arrangements still apply. Identify why you are leaving and how urgent it is An immediate escape from fire or a visibly unsafe building is different from a regional evacuation with preparation time. Do not delay immediate escape to finish a packing checklist. For a developing hazard, confirm the affected area, applicable deadline, current route instructions, and suitable destination while there is still time to arrange support. Departure priorities People Account for the household and required assistance; leave immediate danger without waiting for belongings. Destination and route For a wider evacuation, use current hazard-specific directions and a checked place to arrive. Essentials and contact Take urgent care items and the manageable bag when time permits; report the destination when safe. Editorial planning aid. Actual hazards, access needs and current instructions control the decision. Sheltering can sometimes be the safer action during an airborne chemical or radiation hazard. Do not assume that movement is always protective. Use the specific incident guidance and the actual condition of the building. If the building itself is burning, flooding, or failing, that immediate danger also matters. Confirm a destination that meets the actual needs A destination is usable only if it is reachable, accepting people, and suitable for their needs. Call or use an appropriate current information channel when available. Check the exact address, opening status, entry requirements, accessibility, essential care, pet arrangements, and what supplies people must bring. A map marker is not evidence of admission or medical support. Destination checks before a non-immediate move Check Useful question Location Is it outside the specific hazard area, and is the route currently usable? Acceptance Can the whole household stay, and is acceptance confirmed? Access Can a person use the entrance, toilet, sleeping space, and available movement routes? Care Can necessary equipment, medicine storage, or caregiving continue? Pets Are the actual animals permitted, with suitable transport and supplies? Alternate What is the next realistic option if this location closes or cannot accept you? If emergency conditions prevent confirmation, keep the uncertainty visible in the plan and prioritize the best available protective information. Do not describe a potential shelter as a guaranteed solution to another household member. Plan transport around people, not only bags Count seats, helpers, pets, mobility equipment, care supplies, and bags together. Confirm who drives or provides transport, where pickup happens, and when the arrangement must be used. Someone who can usually use stairs may be unable to do so while carrying equipment or supporting a child. If using a vehicle, preserve fuel or charge and confirm a suitable route. Do not depend on every station being open. For arranged assistance, verify the actual service, registration, eligibility, and pickup arrangements in advance where possible. If there is no car, identify realistic alternatives early rather than waiting until roads or transit are disrupted. Do not assume walking preserves the original plan. Distance, weather, mobility, safe routes, and carryable supplies change the decision. Keep contact and destination information on paper as well as in a device. The Florida county reference illustrates advance zone and transport planning, not rules for every location. Your own community’s arrangements may differ. A registration or a request for help should not be confused with a confirmed immediate pickup. Evacuation without a car Access and mobility needs Use a departure check that does not slow escape For a planned departure with time available, use a short ordered check: people and care, transport and destination, then manageable essentials. Place daily-use medicine and equipment on a grab list so they are not forgotten. Assign tasks without leaving a dependent person alone while every adult searches for supplies. Account for people and pets and identify who assists each person. Check transport, destination, and current route information. Take necessary care items, identification, keys, a light, contacts, suitable water, and the tested bag as time allows. Tell the outside contact where the group is going and when you expect another check-in, when safe. Leave without returning for optional items. Do not enter danger to complete the checklist. Secure the home only when it is safe and does not delay departure. Utility shutoff is not a universal evacuation task; follow the applicable utility or incident instructions and do not manipulate unfamiliar systems. A property checklist belongs below people and care, not above them. If the route or destination changes Do not force the original route through flooded, closed, or actively dangerous roads. Use current route instructions and a safer checked alternative when available. A navigation app may be unaware of the hazard or a closure. If no safer movement is available, compare the immediate danger of staying with the danger of the route and use hazard-specific guidance. Plan changes to rehearse before departure Change Response to prepare First destination is closed Use the suitable alternate and send a change-of-plan message when safe. Vehicle is unavailable Activate the realistic transport alternative; reassess what can be carried. Group becomes separated Use the agreed safe meeting and contact arrangements; do not improvise a hazardous search. Care requirement changes Prioritize the relevant urgent-care or provider-directed plan. An airborne hazard makes travel unsafe Use the specific shelter instruction and reassess; movement is not automatically safer. A useful change message states who is present, the new destination, immediate needs, and the next expected contact. Sending it must not delay getting clear of danger. Keep necessary records private and share the location with trusted people who need it, rather than posting a detailed household route publicly. Arrival, separation, and safe return At arrival, count everyone, settle essential care, and tell the outside contact the actual location when safe. Check sleeping, hygiene, water, and device power arrangements before assuming the journey solved all needs. Confirm who is responsible for children and pets during the stay and how the group will reconnect if someone leaves briefly. Return is a new decision. Use current access and hazard instructions, and do not enter a damaged building or unsafe utility area simply because a road reopens. Think through care, water, food, and sanitation before a non-urgent return. Take the appropriate safe route and avoid making several unnecessary trips through a disrupted area. Keep receipts and useful records of losses and accommodation when appropriate. Replenish the bag and transport reserve after use. Record which destination, route, contact, or carrying assumption failed. Update the household plan using what was actually available, rather than only the original intended arrangement. A safe practice beforehand can test the departure sequence without simulating a hazardous journey. Discuss one route closure and one unavailable destination. The goal is a flexible household plan that another capable adult can use. Make two destinations and more than one route in advance. Keep a small grab list by the door, especially for medications, pets, and items that cannot be prepacked. If a route is unsafe, do not force it. Follow current local instructions or contact emergency services for help. Some hazards, especially radiation fallout, can make immediate travel more dangerous than sheltering; follow the hazard-specific order. Choose a reachable destination with someone you trust, identify a second route, and agree on a check-in. Do not wait for transport that has not been confirmed. If the route is actively dangerous, compare the specific hazard of staying with the hazard of moving; shelter while reassessing if no safer route is available. Give dependents a written contact card and agree who stays with each person. Keep essential medicine and mobility equipment accessible. A pet carrier or heavy bag must not block a caregiver from helping someone move. Evacuation Identify why you are leaving and how urgent it is Confirm a destination that meets the actual needs Plan transport around people, not only bags Use a departure check that does not slow escape If the route or destination changes Arrival, separation, and safe return Confirm the order Check the official zone, deadline, route, shelter options, and whether the order includes your address. Gather people first Account for everyone and pets. Take required medication and medical supplies, documents, accessible equipment, keys, and a charged phone. Do not spend critical time packing extras. Choose a destination Go to a trusted contact or designated shelter outside the hazard area. Check pet rules, accessibility, and transport needs. Leave and report safely Use current official routes. Share your destination with an out-of-area contact, keep fuel in the vehicle if relevant, and do not return until authorities say it is safe.

title: Evacuation with access or mobility needs
summary: Plan movement around the person who needs the most assistance. Keep mobility aids, medicines, communication tools and essential care supplies together. Confirm accessible transport and a suitable destination directly; do not assume a shelter, lift or public rescue vehicle will be available.
text: Plan movement around the person who needs the most assistance. Keep mobility aids, medicines, communication tools and essential care supplies together. Confirm accessible transport and a suitable destination directly; do not assume a shelter, lift or public rescue vehicle will be available.  Does accessible entry mean the destination meets my needs? No. Check toilets, sleeping, communication, power, essential care, assistance and equipment arrangements separately, then verify actual conditions on arrival. Should we practice carrying someone down stairs? Do not improvise an untrained carry. Develop the building-specific plan with the person and appropriate professionals, and rehearse only safe agreed actions. Describe assistance as tasks, with the person’s input Start with what the individual says they need and what safely works for them. A diagnosis alone does not explain how to leave a building, communicate, travel, use a toilet, or maintain essential care. Plan for a difficult day as well as a good one. Pain, fatigue, noise, loss of power and an unfamiliar setting may change what the person can manage independently. A practical assistance record Task Record the real requirement Movement Usable distance, stairs, transfers, mobility aid and safe assistance. Communication Preferred language or format, aid, interpreter or written prompts. Care Prescribed routine, equipment dependencies and care-provider contacts. Transport Suitable vehicle, boarding requirements and equipment space. Destination Entry, toilet, sleeping, charging and caregiver arrangements. Use consent to decide which helpers receive sensitive details. Keep a concise task note available to trusted people without publishing medical records. Ask the care provider or equipment supplier about technical and clinical questions rather than inventing a generic carrying method or backup power rule. Check the entire route, including the building exit A route is only usable if the person can move from their actual starting place to the destination. Check doors, locks, thresholds, corridors, stairs, outside surfaces, pickup position and vehicle boarding. Do this in normal safe conditions with appropriate support. Do not rely on an elevator as the only exit arrangement, especially in a fire, power failure or damaged building. Every part of the route needs a workable answer Building How does the person reach the appropriate safe exit or planned refuge? Transport Who assists, what vehicle fits, and how are the person and equipment moved safely? Destination Can the site support access, communication and essential care on arrival? Editorial planning aid. Actual hazards, individual needs and current instructions control the response. Discuss the site-specific evacuation plan with building management or the responsible fire-safety professional before an emergency. If a refuge is part of that plan, know how assistance is requested and what the arrangement actually provides. Do not assume an unmarked landing is safe for every hazard. Never practice by blocking exits, disabling alarms, or improvising an untrained carry down stairs. Arrange named helpers and transport backups Make the primary helper’s role explicit: check in, reach the person, assist with specified tasks, and communicate the outcome. Ask whether they can realistically reach the location when roads, lifts or phones fail. A nearby relative may face the same disruption. Identify another viable option and keep current contact information for both. A message requesting help is not confirmation that someone is on the way. Ask helpers to learn the person-approved assistance method through suitable training or professional guidance. Confirm who can unlock the location and how lawful access is arranged. Check whether the transport provider can accommodate the actual mobility equipment and necessary companion. Ask any local registry or assistance program about eligibility, registration deadlines, contact procedures and limits; registration is not a rescue guarantee. Decide how the person reports a failed arrangement and the precise assistance still required. Editorial example: a driver offers a car but the required wheelchair will not fit and the person cannot safely transfer. The offer does not complete transport. Resolve the whole journey in advance rather than counting a phone number as a confirmed capability. Recheck when equipment, mobility, helpers or living arrangements change. Keep essential equipment and a useful handover together Write a portable care and equipment note for the person and trusted helper. Include necessary current instructions, contact details, compatible chargers, required consumables, and where daily-use items are kept. Medicines and equipment must be stored and transported under their specific requirements. Use a provider-directed contingency for electricity-dependent care; an ordinary phone power bank does not establish support for a medical device. Separate what travels from what must be grabbed Layer Useful contents or information Always accessible Communication card, trusted contacts and concise assistance preferences. Prepared carry items Suitable charger, approved consumables, spare aids where appropriate. Daily-use grab list Current medicines or equipment that cannot remain packed. Technical instructions Device model, safe operation, power limits and supplier contact. Keep the person with essential mobility or communication aids and a necessary caregiver whenever feasible.
