Agree who will manage children, pets or mobility needs while that action happens. Do not climb a wet or damaged roof to inspect it. Severe storms Leave the open Move into a sturdy building before collecting possessions. Stay away from glass Use an interior room and keep pets inside. If in a car Pull over safely out of traffic, avoid flood-prone areas and remain in the vehicle. Follow other warnings Hail can accompany tornadoes, lightning and strong wind; act on those warnings as well.

title: Heating failure in cold weather
summary: Use dry layers, blankets and a smaller dry room while you identify safe heat or a warmer reachable place. Never use a gas oven, barbecue or generator to heat indoors. Confusion, slurred speech, unusual drowsiness or poor coordination can mean hypothermia: seek urgent care and begin safe warming.
text: Use dry layers, blankets and a smaller dry room while you identify safe heat or a warmer reachable place. Never use a gas oven, barbecue or generator to heat indoors. Confusion, slurred speech, unusual drowsiness or poor coordination can mean hypothermia: seek urgent care and begin safe warming.  What matters before collecting supplies? Use dry layers, blankets and a smaller dry room while you identify safe heat or a warmer reachable place. Never use a gas oven, barbecue or generator to heat indoors. Confusion, slurred speech, unusual drowsiness or poor coordination can mean hypothermia: seek urgent care and begin safe warming. Collect items only if doing so does not delay this action. What should another household member do? Use a second person to handle communication or dependents while the first carries out the immediate action. For heating failure in cold weather, keep the specific hazard in view: Do not give alcohol as a warming method or rub frostbitten skin. Fuel-burning devices can create lethal CO even when you cannot smell anything. What should be written down? Record when the situation changed, what action was taken and what remains uncertain. For this situation, start with: Move before severe exposure. Confirm a warmer destination and safe route while people can still travel. Do not cross dangerous ice or an active hazard merely to reach a public warming centre. Keep personal notes private; they are not submitted to Osprey Zero.  Contact a qualified repair provider when reachable and safe. Plan for medication storage, food, water and sanitation during a longer outage; a portable heater alone does not solve all needs. Do not give alcohol as a warming method or rub frostbitten skin. Fuel-burning devices can create lethal CO even when you cannot smell anything. Use the safest dry shelter and insulation available while confirming a warmer private or community destination. Leave early if you cannot keep vulnerable people warm rather than waiting for official shelter. Assign a trusted adult to each person who needs assistance. Keep medicines, essential contacts and a workable reunion plan with the group. Make decisions around the least mobile person, not the fastest; avoid splitting the family without a clear, safe way to reconnect. For this situation, brief every person on the first action: get dry and insulated. Agree who will manage children, pets or mobility needs while that action happens. Do not give alcohol as a warming method or rub frostbitten skin. Fuel-burning devices can create lethal CO even when you cannot smell anything. no heat heater broken freezing house heating outage Get dry and insulated Replace wet clothes, layer loose dry clothing and insulate beneath the body as well as above it. Keep vulnerable people away from draughts. Use one workable space Choose a dry room that remains safe and has a usable exit. Close unnecessary interior doors without blocking ventilation needed by approved heating appliances. Avoid combustion shortcuts Use only heating equipment approved for indoor use according to its instructions, with working CO alarms. A grill, oven or indoor generator is not a backup heater. Check people regularly Cold can impair judgement. Pay particular attention to infants, older people and anyone with illness or limited mobility. Do not rely on a person saying they feel fine. Move before severe exposure Confirm a warmer destination and safe route while people can still travel. Do not cross dangerous ice or an active hazard merely to reach a public warming centre.

title: Home fire
aliases: there is a fire in my kitchen
summary: Get out, stay out and call emergency services from outside. Use the nearest safe exit, stay low beneath smoke, and close doors behind you if possible. Do not stop for belongings or go back inside for people or pets; tell firefighters where they may be.
text: Can I retrieve a phone or a pet? Do not delay escape or reenter for belongings or animals. Once outside, tell responders where anyone may remain. Keep the household assembly point clear so missing people can be identified without people searching inside. The exit is blocked — what then? Do not force a hot door or a route filling with smoke. Close doors between you and the fire, call and signal your exact location. A high-rise needs its building-specific plan; use the Apartment & high-rise fire guide rather than guessing at an elevator or window escape.  Install and test smoke alarms and practice two ways out with the household. Plan assistance for children and people with mobility needs. An extinguisher attempt must never delay escape or block your exit. Escape immediately, gather outside and keep the exit area clear. If trapped, close the door between you and smoke, signal from a window and send your exact location if possible. Do not reenter because the fire seems quiet or because firefighters have not arrived. Practice the route with children and anyone needing movement assistance. Agree on a nearby meeting point and who will supervise dependents once outside. Include a second safe way out when the building permits it; never block an exit with stored supplies. Fire Leave immediately Follow the escape route and use stairs, not elevators. Check doors for heat before opening; use another exit if unsafe. If the exit is blocked Close doors between you and fire, call emergency services with your location and signal from a window. Meet outside Account for everyone at the meeting point and report missing people to firefighters. Stay outside Do not reenter until the fire department permits it.

title: Home preparedness and practical hardening
summary: Start with working alarms, usable exits, secure doors and windows, and maintenance against local hazards. Hardening should reduce risk while keeping everyone able to escape.
text: Is buying equipment enough? No. Check that it fits the intended task, can be used by the people who need it, and has a maintenance plan. Practice in safe conditions before relying on it. A sensible order of spending Fix a broken exit, alarm or lock before buying specialized equipment. Then address the highest local hazard and the household’s greatest access need. Photograph the baseline, record repairs and keep contractor and insurance information accessible. Cosmetic reinforcement does not establish structural safety. Security without entrapment Do not use traps, electrified barriers or improvised defensive devices. Window bars and additional locks can delay escape or responders; choose lawful systems that occupants can operate in an emergency. Clear sightlines, ordinary lighting and working hardware support everyday security without turning evacuation into a puzzle. Complete a room-by-room audit: one exit issue, one alarm issue, one maintenance issue and one practical security improvement. No home improvement guarantees safety against violent entry or severe weather. Do not remain in a building that has become unsafe because it has been “hardened.” Use the safest usable parts of the home and avoid damaged electrical or structural systems. Where a repair needs a professional, restrict access and relocate if the hazard cannot be controlled; do not improvise structural work during an event. Test locks and exits with the people who actually use them, including those with limited grip, vision or mobility. Store critical equipment at reachable heights. Homes & security home hardening house hardening Audit basic safety Check alarms according to their instructions, keep escape paths clear and identify damaged locks, unsafe wiring, water leaks or blocked drainage. Match improvements to hazards Use local wind, flood, wildfire and heat risks to set priorities. Consult qualified professionals for structural, electrical, roofing or flood-resistant work. Improve access control Repair suitable locks, latch hardware and exterior lighting. Secure outdoor tools and avoid hiding spare keys in obvious places. Preserve safe emergency exit operation. Plan safe occupancy Choose appropriate interior shelter locations for the relevant warning. Keep lights and essential supplies accessible without turning rooms into trip hazards.

title: Household emergency plan
summary: Agree on how to receive warnings, where to shelter, when and where to evacuate, and how to reconnect if separated. Write the plan down and include people who need medication, mobility assistance or caregiver support.
text: How long should the written plan be? Keep the first-action, contact, role and destination information concise. Put equipment manuals and more detailed care information where they can be found separately. Test whether another person can use the plan without the organizer explaining it. What if a helper is unavailable? Name another realistic option and mark any unconfirmed arrangement. Review the person’s essential needs directly; do not make the entire plan depend on a single neighbor or a reply to one message. Start with the household you actually have A useful plan describes who does what when normal arrangements stop working. Begin with the people, pets, places, and services your household relies on. Include anyone who stays part time, someone away at school or work, and a person who may need help communicating or moving. A plan for four fit adults will not work unchanged for a family with a toddler and an adult who cannot use stairs. Build a dependency list before buying equipment Need Write down Fallback to investigate Care Medicines, powered equipment, caregivers, and storage requirements Provider-approved backup and an accessible alternative location. Movement Stairs, transport, keys, mobility aids A second helper or transport arrangement that can actually be reached. Communication Usable devices, languages, hearing or vision needs A written contact card and an agreed accessible contact method. Daily essentials Drinking water, food, toilet arrangements, pets Supplies everyone can use and the point at which home stops working. Make the list short enough to update. Write facts you have checked and mark assumptions that still need work. An advertised shelter, a neighbor’s vehicle, and an electric door are not reliable fallbacks until their limits and availability are understood. Separate immediate escape from planned relocation Choose a nearby meeting point for escaping a home fire and a separate destination for being unable to return to the neighborhood. These serve different purposes. The fire meeting point is where people can be counted after leaving; it is not necessarily somewhere to sleep. A relocation destination needs a safe route, acceptance, and suitable care and access. Three parts of a complete movement plan Get clear Leave immediate danger without collecting belongings. Use the appropriate building escape plan. Account for people Meet at the agreed safe place, count everyone, and communicate any missing person to responders. Continue safely For a wider evacuation, use a checked destination and route, with an alternate if they fail. Editorial planning aid. Actual hazards, access needs and current instructions control the decision. Do not send someone back into a dangerous building to retrieve a bag, pet, or missing person. Tell responders what is known. For a developing regional emergency, preparations can happen before departure becomes urgent: transport, medicines, pets, destination, and an alternate. Keep that longer checklist distinct from immediate escape. Write the contact and reunion rules Choose an out-of-area contact who agrees to the role. Give everyone the same contact information on paper as well as in their devices. Decide what to report: who is with you, your condition, where you are, and when you expect to make contact again. A missed message should trigger an agreed, realistic response rather than an improvised search into danger. Record school or daycare pickup rules, authorized collectors, and where children may be taken if the normal site closes. Agree what a person should do if unable to reach the primary meeting point. The alternative must also be safe for the actual incident. Include helpers who can support access or care needs, with permission to share only the information necessary for the task. Keep address and destination information readable without an internet connection. Protect sensitive records; do not post a household plan publicly. Example: two adults are at work when a neighborhood is evacuated. The plan should explain who can collect the child, where the child will go, and how the other adult learns the new destination. Both adults independently driving to the school can waste time and leave the next decision unclear. Assign tasks and backups without making one person indispensable Distribute tasks by ability and location. One adult can manage a dependent person while another checks transport and communicates. Someone living alone can still assign an outside check-in contact and keep the essentials organized for self-use. Avoid a plan that requires the only person away at work to come home before any action can begin. A compact task sheet Task Primary person Backup or limit Support each dependent Name the adult and the specific assistance Identify an alternative; do not assume neighbors are available. Transport and destination Name the driver or transport contact Record another realistic option and when to switch. Contacts and updates Name the information person Keep the paper list accessible to another adult. Essentials Name who keeps bags and daily-use grab list ready Never let packing delay immediate escape. Give tasks clear end points. “Handle the pets” is less useful than “put each pet in its labelled carrier and bring its medicine.” Keep a paper location list for daily-use items that cannot live in a bag. Do not give children responsibility for fuel, electrical work, or decisions about whether a building is safe. Set decision triggers before an emergency A trigger states the condition that changes the plan and the action that follows. Use conditions you can recognize: an applicable evacuation order, an unsafe building, an essential device losing backup, or the inability to maintain safe water and sanitation. A vague promise to “leave if things get bad” gives a tired household too much to debate. List the local hazards that could require leaving and those that may require sheltering. The correct response depends on the hazard. For care and equipment, use provider and manufacturer limits. Do not invent a general battery percentage that applies to every person. Choose a time to review stable conditions, but act immediately if an urgent danger develops. Record what information would change a decision, where it comes from, and what you can do if that channel fails. For an editorial example, a household may decide to relocate while transport remains available if it cannot sustain a particular care need at home. That threshold belongs to the individual care plan. A restoration estimate or social-media rumor should not silently replace it. Staying home with exit limits Evacuation planning Test the plan with a realistic tabletop exercise Gather the people who use the plan and choose one scenario: power fails while one adult is away and phones are unreliable. Ask each person to explain the next action, not simply agree that the plan looks sensible. Keep essential equipment operating; this exercise is discussion and safe practice, not a deliberate loss of medical support. Locate the contact card, light, medicines grab list, keys, and relevant bag without turning the exercise into a race. Describe the first check-in and the response if it cannot be delivered. Check the destination and route assumptions, including pets and access. Introduce one change: the driver is unavailable, a road is closed, or the destination cannot accept everyone. Write down the first three problems and fix the most consequential one before adding more equipment. Review after moving, a new medical need, a change of school, a new pet, or a different caregiver. Put the review date on the plan and retire confusing old copies. Success means another household member can explain and carry out the plan, not that the folder is impressive. Keep copies offline and in go bags. Share relevant details with caregivers and trusted contacts. A plan that depends on one vehicle or one working phone network needs alternatives. Give each household member a written copy with two meeting places, two contacts and essential medical details. Practise the plan with phones off. Include a destination you can actually reach without an official shelter or rescue transport. Write the plan in formats everyone can use: plain text, large print, translated wording or another needed communication format. Ask each person which assistance they want. Store private identity and health details securely rather than in public shared links. Planning Start with the household you actually have Separate immediate escape from planned relocation Write the contact and reunion rules Assign tasks and backups without making one person indispensable Set decision triggers before an emergency Test the plan with a realistic tabletop exercise Identify local risks Use local emergency management information and plan for likely hazards. Choose meeting places Pick a nearby safe place and an out-of-area destination plus backup routes. Assign contact arrangements Name an out-of-area contact, write phone numbers and agree on check-in times. Practice and update Run a simple drill and revise for changes in health, school, work or pets.

title: Household inventory: what you own, what works and what is missing
summary: A useful inventory records usable supplies, condition, location and next action. Count what works for your actual household instead of turning preparedness into an endless shopping list.
text: Is buying equipment enough? No. Check that it fits the intended task, can be used by the people who need it, and has a maintenance plan. Practice in safe conditions before relying on it. Quantity is not duration Duration depends on people, pets, climate, actual use and safe storage. Calculate water and meal requirements separately and avoid a single readiness percentage that hides a failing essential. Record consumables alongside any equipment that needs them. Location is part of inventory Write where supplies are stored and how they can be accessed in low light or without lifts. Keep exits and equipment ventilation clear. Split portable items from home reserves and keep urgent medicines or support information readily reachable. Inventory one shelf and one essential device today, then complete the highest-priority missing action. Do not count expired, damaged or incompatible supplies as usable. Avoid heavy storage that creates injury or blocked exits. Use a notebook or a simple spreadsheet if an app is unavailable. Update quantities when supplies are used. A basic accurate record is more useful than an elaborate dashboard full of old data. Include allergies, mobility aids, pets, infants and the needs of people who visit or provide care. Do not expose sensitive records on a shared device without discussing access. Planning inventory stockpile supplies Start with essentials Record water, food, medication arrangements, lighting, communications, hygiene, care equipment and portable departure supplies. Test usability Check dates, batteries, cable compatibility, labels, container condition and who knows how to operate equipment. A broken or inaccessible item is not a reliable reserve. Record a clear next action Give each gap a practical action, owner, cost estimate and due date. Prioritize essential needs and access issues. Review at a manageable interval Check after use, a household change or an approaching local hazard season. Keep a routine simple enough to maintain.

title: Household preparedness drills that reveal real gaps
summary: Use short, safe rehearsals to test actual people, equipment and decisions. Improve one weak step at a time rather than staging dangerous surprise emergencies.
text: Is buying equipment enough? No. Check that it fits the intended task, can be used by the people who need it, and has a maintenance plan. Practice in safe conditions before relying on it. A simple monthly rotation Rotate a short contact check, supply-date review, departure rehearsal and safe equipment familiarization session. Keep the schedule manageable so it survives normal life. Record an action completed, not just a readiness score. A checklist full of untested assumptions does not establish capability. Include failure deliberately Try a unavailable driver, a phone with no signal or a forgotten charger in a controlled setting. Ask which alternative is usable without help. Do not simulate hazards by actually disabling safety systems or blocking exits. A drill should make the household calmer and more capable, not frightened or exhausted. Choose one ten-minute drill this week and complete its single highest-value improvement before scheduling the next. Never stage surprise armed scenarios, real smoke exposure, dangerous driving or deprivation exercises. Practice the protective steps you can complete independently. Keep a short paper plan so the exercise does not require internet, a paid app or a responding service to succeed. Adapt drills to age, disability, language and anxiety. Use predictable steps, consent and breaks. Record where help is needed rather than labeling someone as the problem. Practice & maintenance Pick one scenario Choose departure, a communications failure or locating equipment in low light. State the objective and stop conditions before starting. Protect essential care Do not disconnect necessary medical equipment, withhold medicines or create hazardous heat, cold, smoke or fire. Tell participants it is a drill. Use real equipment Try the actual bags, chargers, contacts and accessible routes. Note missing adapters, forgotten keys, unclear roles and uncomfortable carrying loads. Review and fix Ask what worked, what failed and one concrete change. Assign an owner and a date, then repeat only the affected part.

title: Hurricane
summary: Check your evacuation zone and the current order. If told to evacuate, leave before conditions deteriorate. If staying outside an evacuation zone, shelter inside a sturdy building away from windows; storm surge and inland flooding can be deadly even far from the storm center.
text: What matters before collecting supplies? Check your evacuation zone and the current order. If told to evacuate, leave before conditions deteriorate. If staying outside an evacuation zone, shelter inside a sturdy building away from windows; storm surge and inland flooding can be deadly even far from the storm center. Collect items only if doing so does not delay this action. What should another household member do? Use a second person to handle communication or dependents while the first carries out the immediate action. For hurricane, keep the specific hazard in view: A calm eye is not an all-clear. Do not base flood safety on the wind category. What should be written down? Record when the situation changed, what action was taken and what remains uncertain. For this situation, start with: Watch for water. Keep out of flooded roads and basements. Follow separate flash-flood warnings and move to safer higher ground when necessary. Keep personal notes private; they are not submitted to Osprey Zero.  Expect extended outages. Store water, protect documents and charge devices before the storm. Return only after officials allow reentry. A calm eye is not an all-clear. Do not base flood safety on the wind category. Before roads become unsafe, move out of surge-prone areas using a route and destination you have checked. If already trapped by wind or water, stay in the safest intact interior space available, with flood risk in mind. Do not travel during the calm eye. Account for children, older people, pets and anyone who needs assistance before moving. Keep shoes, medicines and a torch in the shelter area. Decide who helps whom and who carries the essential supplies; do not send a lone child to retrieve items. For this situation, brief every person on the first action: check your zone. Agree who will manage children, pets or mobility needs while that action happens. A calm eye is not an all-clear. Do not base flood safety on the wind category. Tropical weather Check your zone Read local evacuation and storm-surge instructions for your address, not just the forecast track. Leave when directed Use official routes to a destination outside the hazard area. Bring medications, identification, pets and phone power. Shelter for wind If the building is safe and evacuation is not required, stay in an interior room away from windows during strong winds. Watch for water Keep out of flooded roads and basements. Follow separate flash-flood warnings and move to safer higher ground when necessary.

title: Hygiene with limited water
summary: Reserve safe water for drinking, food, medicines and essential hygiene. Wash hands with safe water and soap before food preparation and after toilet or waste handling. Keep clean and dirty tasks separate. Sanitiser with at least 60% alcohol helps when hands are not visibly dirty; it does not remove chemicals or replace washing dirty hands.
text: Reserve safe water for drinking, food, medicines and essential hygiene. Wash hands with safe water and soap before food preparation and after toilet or waste handling. Keep clean and dirty tasks separate. Sanitiser with at least 60% alcohol helps when hands are not visibly dirty; it does not remove chemicals or replace washing dirty hands.  Can sanitizer replace every wash? No. CDC notes that sanitizer has limits, including visibly dirty or greasy hands and harmful chemicals. Plan suitable water and soap, especially around toilet, waste and meal tasks. Can I use water that is unsafe to drink for bathing? Sometimes an advisory allows certain non-drinking uses, but it depends on the contaminant and notice. Follow the specific permission; do not infer it from a different incident. Build a clean-to-dirty workflow When water, drainage, and rubbish collection fail, hygiene is a household system rather than a bottle of sanitizer. Decide where clean drinking water and food stay, where people wash hands, where personal care happens, and how waste is contained. Keep these activities separate enough that a dirty container, glove, or cloth cannot routinely pass through the meal area. A simple hygiene workflow Clean supplies Keep safe water, food, clean care items, and utensils protected. Handwashing Use an accessible dispensing point with appropriate water and soap, and a suitable way to handle runoff. Waste and used items Keep contained waste and soiled materials separate; wash hands before returning to clean tasks. Editorial layout concept. It is not a plumbing or waste-disposal design; local water and sanitation restrictions still apply. In a small dwelling, separation may mean labelled containers, a dedicated changing surface, and a sequence that is easy to follow rather than different rooms. Choose a stable setup the least mobile person can use. Keep walking routes clear, particularly at night. Waste should not be placed where children or pets can access it. Handwashing is the priority CDC advises washing hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds. Important times include after toilet use or handling waste and before preparing or eating food. Check the actual water advisory to determine whether tap water is acceptable for handwashing; a drinking restriction and a do-not-use restriction are different. Match the method to the conditions Condition Practical response Suitable water and soap available Use proper handwashing and a clean drying method. No normal running tap Set up a stable jug dispenser with appropriate water; avoid shared dipping into the supply. Soap and water unavailable CDC identifies sanitizer containing at least 60% alcohol as an alternative in some situations. Visibly dirty or greasy hands Sanitizer is less effective; obtain soap and appropriate water. Possible chemical contamination Sanitizer may not remove harmful chemicals; follow exposure guidance rather than assuming it decontaminates. Keep soap and a light beside the station rather than in a separate cupboard. Plan where runoff goes; do not use drains affected by sewage failure. Teach the setup to children with suitable supervision and arrange assistance for anyone who cannot operate the dispenser. Empty or unstable equipment creates a station that exists on paper but not in practice. Use limited water for essential personal care Choose suitable water for brushing teeth and follow the local notice for bathing. Do not bathe in water potentially contaminated with sewage or toxic chemicals. Reduced bathing can be a practical temporary adjustment, but necessary handwashing, oral care, and provider-directed care still need a plan. Keep each person’s toothbrush, hygiene items, and drying materials identifiable; do not make several people share a dirty cloth. Plan menstrual supplies, continence care, skin care, and privacy explicitly rather than calling all of these “toiletries.” Record special water or cleaning requirements from an individual care plan. A general household routine does not replace those instructions. Keep wounds protected from contaminated water, and seek medical help for signs of infection or other concerning change. Separate pet cleanup from human meal and personal-care surfaces. Estimate water used by an actual routine rather than making an arbitrary ration. Try a safe practice while normal water remains available: locate supplies, operate the dispenser, and complete the usual essential tasks. Use the observed amount to improve the reserve. Never withhold necessary drinking water or prescribed care to make a target last longer. Diapering and assisted care need their own setup Prepare a dedicated, cleanable changing area away from food. Bring the required items before starting so the child is not left unattended while a caregiver searches. Follow CDC’s diaper-changing sequence, including separating soiled items, washing the child’s hands, cleaning and disinfecting the surface as directed, and washing the caregiver’s hands. Use an appropriate product for the surface and follow its label, including any contact time. Disposable gloves, when used, do not replace handwashing. Keep clean diapers, wipes, spare clothes, and bagging materials within reach, while putting the closed used-item container where children cannot reach it. Adult continence care also needs dignity, a stable position, privacy, and any individual skin-care instructions. Plan the whole care cycle A stack of clean diapers is only one part of the plan. Include the changing space, handwashing water, cleaning supplies, soiled-clothing containment, waste route, and a backup caregiver if needed. If a caregiver must also prepare meals, make the transition explicit: finish the dirty task, contain used items, clean as directed, wash hands, then return to clean supplies. Do not put a changing mat on the only meal-preparation surface just because it is convenient. Cleaning is different from disinfecting Cleaning removes visible soil; disinfecting uses a suitable product as directed to address germs. Product type, surface, and instructions matter. Do not mix cleaning chemicals or improvise concentrated recipes. A chemical label must be readable and the product kept out of drinking-water containers. An editorial cleaning checklist Step What to verify Identify the surface and contamination Ordinary household dirt, a changing surface, and sewage contamination need different responses. Choose a suitable product Read the label for permitted surfaces, dilution, precautions, and contact time. Prepare the work area Keep food, people needing care, and pets away from the dirty task. Handle used materials Keep soiled cloths and waste separate from clean supplies. Finish safely Wash hands and restore clean supplies without recontaminating them. Significant sewage contamination may require qualified cleanup and an alternative living space. Do not treat a quick wipe or a splash of bleach as proof that a contaminated room is safe. Keep electrical and structural hazards in view, and avoid entering unsafe water to begin cleaning. Sewer failure and temporary toilets Maintain the routine and know its limits Record suitable water, soap, personal-care consumables, liners, and the functioning waste route. Review actual use and replenish before the routine fails. A supply of waste bags does not establish that collection exists or that every type of waste can go into ordinary rubbish. Follow the relevant local disposal arrangements. Check the station at the start of the day: water, soap, light, stability, and runoff arrangements. Check each person’s essential personal-care needs and the supplies they can actually use. Keep clean and used materials separated, and supervise children appropriately. Record any service or advisory change and adjust the routine. If safe water, care, or waste containment cannot be sustained, arrange a suitable alternative location early. After normal service returns, confirm the appropriate water and drainage instructions, clean affected equipment as directed, and replenish the hygiene kit. Note one preventable difficulty: a missing soap dispenser, an inaccessible container, inadequate privacy, or an unconfirmed waste route. Fixing that difficulty can provide more value than buying another generic emergency pouch. Replenish safe water when a verified source becomes available. Keep a routine that the household can sustain; a simple clean station is more useful than occasional improvised deep cleaning. Surface disinfectant is not drinking-water treatment. Do not apply household bleach to skin or mix bleach with ammonia or other cleaners. Use the smallest workable clean-water station and protect it from contamination. Reduce nonessential washing before cutting drinking water or essential handwashing. Make the hygiene plan usable for children, mobility needs and caregivers changing diapers or handling wounds. Keep gloves, cleaning tools and drinking-water supplies distinct. Tell everyone where the clean handwashing area is and who manages waste. no running water hygiene wash hands outage limited water sanitation Build a clean-to-dirty workflow Handwashing is the priority Use limited water for essential personal care Diapering and assisted care need their own setup Cleaning is different from disinfecting Maintain the routine and know its limits Set up a clean station Put safe water, soap and a clean towel or air-drying arrangement near food and care tasks. Use a container that does not require everyone to dip dirty hands into the supply. Prioritise key washing times Wash after toilet and waste handling, before eating or preparing food and before wound or infant care. Do not use suspected chemically contaminated water on skin. Use sanitiser appropriately Use at least 60% alcohol sanitiser when soap and safe water are unavailable and hands are not visibly dirty. Keep it away from flames and children. Separate waste and food Store rubbish and toilet waste away from water, food and sleeping areas. Clean high-contact surfaces using product instructions without mixing chemicals. Plan personal care Include menstrual supplies, nappies, necessary skin care and clean clothing. Keep wounds clean and covered; worsening redness, pain or fever needs medical assessment.

title: Ice storm
summary: Avoid travel on icy roads and keep away from ice-laden trees and power lines. Prepare for a long outage using safe heat and battery lights. Stay indoors until conditions improve unless your shelter is unsafe.
text: What matters before collecting supplies? Avoid travel on icy roads and keep away from ice-laden trees and power lines. Prepare for a long outage using safe heat and battery lights. Stay indoors until conditions improve unless your shelter is unsafe. Collect items only if doing so does not delay this action. What should another household member do? Use a second person to handle communication or dependents while the first carries out the immediate action. For ice storm, keep the specific hazard in view: Never touch or approach a fallen wire, even if it appears inactive. What should be written down? Record when the situation changed, what action was taken and what remains uncertain. For this situation, start with: Check vulnerable people. Plan safe transport to a warm location if heat or essential medical power fails. Keep personal notes private; they are not submitted to Osprey Zero.  Use footwear with traction for necessary movement and do not enter areas beneath damaged trees. Never touch or approach a fallen wire, even if it appears inactive. Preserve heat in a dry room, keep lights battery powered and avoid unnecessary travel. If you must move because of dangerous cold, do it before people become weak and use a route you know is passable; a car is not reliable shelter if exhaust or roads are blocked. Account for children, older people, pets and anyone who needs assistance before moving. Keep shoes, medicines and a torch in the shelter area. Decide who helps whom and who carries the essential supplies; do not send a lone child to retrieve items. For this situation, brief every person on the first action: postpone travel. Agree who will manage children, pets or mobility needs while that action happens. Never touch or approach a fallen wire, even if it appears inactive. Winter Postpone travel Even thin ice can make roads and sidewalks unsafe. Avoid falling hazards Stay clear of branches, wires and roofs shedding ice. Use safe backup heat Keep combustion equipment outdoors and maintain working CO alarms. Check vulnerable people Plan safe transport to a warm location if heat or essential medical power fails.

title: Infant choking
summary: For a baby under one year who cannot cry, cough effectively or breathe, request emergency help and alternate 5 back blows with 5 chest thrusts. Support the head and neck; never give abdominal thrusts to an infant. If unresponsive, begin infant CPR.
text: Blockage clears Stop thrusts when effective coughing, crying or breathing returns. Continue observing and obtain assessment after serious symptoms. An infant is unresponsive Use Child & infant CPR. Responsive choking thrusts are not the CPR technique. Can I put a finger in the mouth? Only remove an object that is clearly visible. A blind sweep can push it further in.  Seek medical assessment after thrusts, persistent cough, breathing changes or any loss of responsiveness. Review what caused the blockage and safe feeding practices. An infant is under one year. AHA’s 2025 heel-of-hand update differs from older two-finger choking materials; use current training. Do not hang a baby upside down or shake them. Begin the sequence immediately while a helper calls. If alone, use speakerphone if reachable without delay. If the infant becomes unresponsive, change to CPR rather than continuing responsive choking care. A delayed responder is not a reason to pause. Have a second caregiver locate help and open access while the first provides care. Teach every regular caregiver the infant sequence using hands-on training; older-child abdominal thrusts are not appropriate for babies. Keep small objects and age-inappropriate food out of reach.  Check for an effective cough A baby who can cough or cry should be watched closely. Do not begin thrusts while the cough remains effective. Give 5 back blows Support the baby face-down on your forearm, braced on your thigh, with the head lower than the chest. Give 5 firm blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand. Give 5 chest thrusts Turn face-up while supporting the head and neck, keeping the head lower. The 2025 AHA update uses the heel of one hand for infant chest thrusts. Alternate with back blows until relieved or unresponsive. Change to CPR if unresponsive Place on a firm flat surface and begin infant CPR. Before breaths, remove an object only if clearly visible. Never sweep the mouth blindly.

title: Infants & children during disruption
summary: Keep children with a trusted caregiver and plan safe feeding, water, hygiene, medicines and warmth around their age and needs. Put written contacts with each child and agree a reunion plan. Use age-appropriate feeding guidance; do not dilute formula or use unsafe water to stretch supplies.
text: Keep children with a trusted caregiver and plan safe feeding, water, hygiene, medicines and warmth around their age and needs. Put written contacts with each child and agree a reunion plan. Use age-appropriate feeding guidance; do not dilute formula or use unsafe water to stretch supplies.  Can I dilute formula to make it last longer? No. Follow the product and qualified care instructions. If safe supplies or preparation are unavailable, seek verified feeding support; do not improvise dilution or homemade replacements. Is a well-stocked adult kit enough for an infant? No. Feeding, cleaning, storage, hygiene, transport, sleep and caregiver arrangements need their own child-specific plan and usable supplies. Build around one ordinary day of care List what each child uses in an ordinary day: feeding, drinking, hygiene, medicines, communication, sleep and safe transport. Then identify which tasks depend on clean water, electricity, refrigeration, a particular adult or a school. Infants, toddlers and teenagers need different plans. Do not apply an adult pantry or water calculation as a complete infant-care plan. A child-specific planning sheet Need Record Check before relying on it Feeding Usual product or method and relevant care instructions. Safe preparation, cleaning and storage during disruption. Care Prescribed medicines, aids and individual requirements. Current instructions, suitable storage and backup support. Supervision Named caregiver and trusted backup. Pickup permission and how the handover is confirmed. Comfort and communication Useful routine, language and familiar items. What the child understands and can safely do. Movement Appropriate transport or carrier arrangement. Fit, use instructions and actual space with the family’s bags. Write the information so the backup adult can use it. Keep product names and care instructions specific where needed, and separate private records from a simple contact card. Review quantities as the child grows rather than leaving an old diaper bag labelled emergency-ready indefinitely. Protect the feeding method instead of improvising substitutes CDC identifies ready-to-feed infant formula as the safest formula option during emergencies because it does not need mixing water. If formula is used, check suitable products, supply and storage with the child’s needs in mind. Follow label instructions after opening and feeding; unopened shelf stability does not make an opened container safe indefinitely. Do not dilute formula, make homemade replacements or change prescribed feeding without qualified advice. Powdered formula needs a separate safe plan It requires appropriate safe water, correct preparation and clean feeding equipment. If it is the only available option, use CDC’s specific guidance and seek qualified feeding support. A general camping water treatment instruction is not an infant-feeding protocol. If breastfeeding or expressing milk, plan access to appropriate support and any necessary equipment, cleaning and storage. A powered pump introduces dependencies that direct feeding may not have; discuss a workable backup with a qualified lactation provider. Do not assume stress automatically stops milk production or that an unfamiliar feeding technique can safely be learned from a hurried improvisation. Separate feeding, diapering and clean storage Organize care supplies by clean and soiled tasks. Keep the feeding area and equipment separate from diaper waste, cleaning chemicals and contaminated belongings. Use safe water and appropriate cleaning instructions for reusable feeding items. A packet of wipes does not replace every cleaning step required by a bottle or pump. If the required cleaning cannot be done, seek a suitable supported alternative rather than repeatedly reusing contaminated equipment. Keep age-appropriate feeding supplies and their instructions together, with a plan for opened items. Place diapers, suitable personal-care items, clean clothing and waste containment in a separate clearly marked group. Use a dedicated clean storage arrangement for prepared feeding equipment. Record where suitable handwashing water and soap are available. Keep product instructions and clinician-directed medicine information readable; do not estimate doses from an adult product. Editorial example: a family packs enough formula but forgets the equipment and water needed to clean its reusable bottles. The food quantity alone does not support feeding. Walk through one complete feed and one change in normal conditions to identify the missing task. Keep normal care available throughout this exercise. Keep a trusted caregiver and a clear handover Assign who stays with each child during sheltering, departure and arrival. A child should not be left alone while an adult searches for supplies or signal. Keep a trusted backup and current school or childcare pickup permissions. Record the expected destination and how another household adult learns it. Avoid two collectors arriving independently while nobody maintains the contact plan. A simple caregiver handover Confirm Identify the trusted responsible adult and authorized collection arrangement. Equip Provide essential care items, current instructions and a minimal contact card. Report Confirm the child’s location, caregiver and next check-in to the household contact. Editorial planning aid. Actual hazards, individual needs and current instructions control the response. Teach an older child the agreed trusted contacts and an age-appropriate separation response without placing adult responsibility on them. Keep sensitive identity and medical details off visible public labels. A child with communication or sensory needs may need a particular format, familiar aid, or calm explanation. Tell the backup caregiver what actually works instead of describing the child only by a diagnosis. Plan safe arrival, rest and a manageable routine Before relocation, ask what the destination can support for the child: safe feeding, suitable sleeping arrangements, essential care, hygiene, temperature and a caregiver. Do not assume an evacuation site has infant supplies merely because families can enter. Keep an appropriate transport arrangement and follow the child-restraint or carrier instructions; emergency travel is not a reason to improvise unsafe restraint. Arrival check before settling Area Question to answer Caregiver Who has direct responsibility right now? Feeding Can the usual safe plan continue with available supplies and equipment? Rest Is there a safe age-appropriate sleeping arrangement? Hygiene Where are clean care tasks done and waste contained? Communication Does the household contact know the confirmed location? Use simple truthful explanations: what is happening now, where the trusted adult is, and the next step. A familiar story, quiet activity or comfort object may help preserve routine. Avoid promises about when danger ends or repeated exposure to frightening media. Ask qualified child-health support about concerning illness or changes rather than treating this planning guide as a diagnostic checklist. Test quantities and identify the first care gap Inventory supplies against actual use and review them when needs change. For a child using a particular formula or prescribed item, count only suitable usable stock. Keep a daily-use grab list for items that cannot remain in the bag. Check expiration, storage and preparation instructions, and replace supplies used during normal life. A large bag with the wrong sizes or products is not an adequate reserve. Walk through a normal care period with the backup adult. Identify water, power, refrigeration and cleaning dependencies. Check the carry load while accounting for who holds or assists the child. Confirm the destination’s care arrangements and pickup permissions. Write the first essential gap and the safe action to resolve it. Recheck the plan after growth, a care change, travel or supply use. If disruption already prevents safe feeding or necessary care, seek verified qualified assistance promptly while keeping the child with a trusted caregiver. Do not stretch supplies through unsafe dilution or borrow someone else’s treatment instructions. Use a suitable alternative location if available and confirmed. The purpose of the reserve is to preserve care and time to act, not to justify waiting through a worsening situation. Family reunification Emergency hygiene Plan quantities for the actual feeding and care routine, and ask a qualified clinician for special dietary or medical needs. Include medications and transport or sleeping arrangements. Infants can deteriorate quickly with dehydration, temperature exposure or illness. Seek qualified care for concerning symptoms; do not rely on adult treatment advice. Use the caregiver plan and safe supplies already available while seeking verified medical or feeding support. Do not stretch formula with extra water or leave a child alone to find supplies. Name the caregiver and trusted backup for each child. Preserve safe feeding and care, keep children supervised during supply searches, and make communication and handovers appropriate to age and individual needs. baby emergency children war infant supplies formula outage Build around one ordinary day of care Protect the feeding method instead of improvising substitutes Separate feeding, diapering and clean storage Keep a trusted caregiver and a clear handover Plan safe arrival, rest and a manageable routine Test quantities and identify the first care gap Name the caregiver Decide who stays with each child during sheltering and travel. Use a familiar trusted backup; do not hand children to unverified helpers. Protect feeding Maintain breastfeeding where applicable. Ready-to-feed formula can avoid preparation water needs when available; follow product and age-specific guidance. Do not improvise formula or change dilution. Keep hygiene supplies Pack nappies, wipes, soap, clean clothing and safe water for essential care. Keep feeding equipment clean and separate from waste. Keep a contact card Use necessary caregiver contact details and medical information without displaying sensitive identity details publicly. Teach older children the agreed safe contacts. Use simple explanations Explain the next action calmly and specifically. Familiar routines and a comfort item can help; avoid promising that you know when danger will end.

title: Knives, saws and hand tools: useful skills, safe limits
summary: Choose tools for a defined task, learn their instructions and keep cutting work separate from people. Tools are part of practical preparedness; they should not add avoidable injuries or become improvised weapons.
text: Is buying equipment enough? No. Check that it fits the intended task, can be used by the people who need it, and has a maintenance plan. Practice in safe conditions before relying on it. A compact repair kit Start with the tools needed to maintain your existing equipment: suitable fasteners, manufacturer-approved repair materials, a small screwdriver set and a practical cutting tool if trained to use it. A larger blade or axe is not automatically more useful. Carrying weight, skill, permitted use and injury consequences all matter. Protect the whole work session Check what is behind or under the material, who can enter the area and how a tool will be put down safely. Gloves may help for an appropriate task but do not make poor technique safe. Never improvise load-bearing repairs, cut live electrical equipment or use a tool in a way the manufacturer prohibits. Inspect a small tool kit, identify one damaged item and arrange a supervised lesson for one useful task. This guide does not cover combat use, weapon construction, traps or hazardous field surgery. Specific cutting techniques need practical instruction. Stop the job if adequate light, footing or competent instruction is unavailable. Use a simpler existing solution or arrange qualified help; finishing a repair is not worth an avoidable serious injury. Keep tools away from shared food and children’s bags. Choose accessible handles and suitable task roles rather than assuming everyone can safely use the same tool. Tools & training knife weapons safety tools Choose the task and tool Use a purpose-made tool of manageable size. Check handles, guards, locking mechanisms and condition; retire damaged equipment rather than relying on tape to restore safety. Set a controlled work area Use stable footing, adequate light and a secure work surface. Keep other people away from the working area and stop when distracted or fatigued. Carry and store safely Use the correct sheath or guard. Secure tools during transport and keep them inaccessible to children. Do not leave blades loose in bags. Learn with supervision Get practical instruction for the actual task. Practice on suitable material in safe conditions before taking a tool on a trip.

title: Landslide & debris flow
summary: Move away from a slide area if you can do so safely, and obey evacuation warnings. Avoid steep slopes, channels and places downhill from recent burns during heavy rain. Do not cross moving debris or enter a fresh slide to inspect it.
text: What matters before collecting supplies? Move away from a slide area if you can do so safely, and obey evacuation warnings. Avoid steep slopes, channels and places downhill from recent burns during heavy rain. Do not cross moving debris or enter a fresh slide to inspect it. Collect items only if doing so does not delay this action. What should another household member do? Use a second person to handle communication or dependents while the first carries out the immediate action. For landslide & debris flow, keep the specific hazard in view: Another slide can follow the first, especially during continued rain. What should be written down? Record when the situation changed, what action was taken and what remains uncertain. For this situation, start with: Report from safety. Give the location and visible hazards to emergency services; keep others out. Keep personal notes private; they are not submitted to Osprey Zero.  Return only after local authorities assess stability. Contact a qualified professional about slope or structural damage. Another slide can follow the first, especially during continued rain. Stay away from channels, fresh debris and unstable slopes after the first movement. Do not cross the slide to check a house or search for belongings. Choose a destination outside the runout area rather than simply a higher point on the same unstable slope. Account for children, older people, pets and anyone who needs assistance before moving. Keep shoes, medicines and a torch in the shelter area. Decide who helps whom and who carries the essential supplies; do not send a lone child to retrieve items. For this situation, brief every person on the first action: notice warning signs. Agree who will manage children, pets or mobility needs while that action happens. Another slide can follow the first, especially during continued rain. Geological Notice warning signs New ground cracks, tilting trees, unusual runoff or rumbling warrant immediate caution and a call to local authorities. Leave the affected area Use an official safe route rather than following a drainage channel. Avoid crossings Mud and debris can sweep away vehicles and hide damaged road surfaces. Report from safety Give the location and visible hazards to emergency services; keep others out.

title: Lightning
summary: When you hear thunder, move into a substantial building or enclosed hard-top vehicle immediately. There is no safe place outdoors during a thunderstorm. Wait at least 30 minutes after the last thunder before going back out.
text: Thunder is audible? Move into a substantial building or enclosed hard-top vehicle immediately. Only a tent or open shelter is nearby? It is not safe lightning shelter. Reduce exposure while heading to a suitable shelter; no outdoor posture removes the risk. The storm seems to have passed? Remain in safe shelter for at least 30 minutes after the last thunder. What matters before collecting supplies? When you hear thunder, move into a substantial building or enclosed hard-top vehicle immediately. There is no safe place outdoors during a thunderstorm. Wait at least 30 minutes after the last thunder before going back out. Collect items only if doing so does not delay this action. What should another household member do? Use a second person to handle communication or dependents while the first carries out the immediate action. For lightning, keep the specific hazard in view: Lightning can strike beyond rainfall. Do not wait for rain to seek shelter. What should be written down? Record when the situation changed, what action was taken and what remains uncertain. For this situation, start with: Help a struck person. Call emergency services. A lightning victim carries no electrical charge; give CPR if needed and follow dispatcher instructions. Keep personal notes private; they are not submitted to Osprey Zero. Plan the shelter before the activity Editorial planning: identify the nearest substantial building or enclosed hard-top vehicle before heading onto a beach, field or trail. Include the time needed for children or anyone with mobility needs to reach it. Choose an earlier cancellation point when the route to shelter is long; do not wait for the group to become trapped far from cover. Check forecasts before outdoor activity and identify shelter before leaving it. Lightning can strike beyond rainfall. Do not wait for rain to seek shelter. Choose a substantial building or enclosed hard-top vehicle now. A tent, tree or open-sided shelter is not protective. If no shelter is available, reduce exposure while moving toward one; there is no outdoor posture that makes lightning safe. Account for children, older people, pets and anyone who needs assistance before moving. Keep shoes, medicines and a torch in the shelter area. Decide who helps whom and who carries the essential supplies; do not send a lone child to retrieve items. For this situation, brief every person on the first action: leave exposed areas. Agree who will manage children, pets or mobility needs while that action happens. Lightning can strike beyond rainfall. Do not wait for rain to seek shelter. Severe storms Leave exposed areas Get out of water and off ridges, fields and beaches. Do not shelter beneath a lone tree. Choose real shelter Use a building or enclosed hard-top vehicle; picnic shelters and tents are not adequate. Avoid indoor pathways Stay away from showers, sinks, corded phones and plugged-in equipment. Help a struck person Call emergency services. A lightning victim carries no electrical charge; give CPR if needed and follow dispatcher instructions.

title: Lithium battery safety: power banks, tools and e-bikes
summary: Follow the device and charger instructions. Stop using a battery with swelling, leakage, unusual heat, odor or noises. If it is smoking or burning, leave the area and call emergency services from a safe place; do not carry it through the home. Keep charging areas away from your escape route.
text: Ordinary inspection finds damage? Stop use and arrange qualified advice. Smoke or fire? Leave, stay out and alert emergency services from a safe location. Can I fix a swollen battery? Do not puncture, compress or open it. Stop using it and seek appropriate handling instructions. Make a household charging map Editorial exercise: list where phones, power banks, tools and mobility batteries are normally charged. Mark any location that blocks a doorway or stair. Move routine charging to a suitable clear area according to the manufacturer; agree who checks that the right charger is used. Buying backup power Compare the jobs you actually need a battery to do, cable compatibility, storage instructions and reputable certification information. Record the model and support contact. A larger battery adds cost and storage needs; test the smallest suitable option before expanding. Review charging locations, remove incompatible chargers from routine use and ask your local collection service about disposal arrangements. A battery exposed to flooding may need specialist handling. Do not test it by charging. Smoke and fire can make the surrounding air unsafe. If a damaged battery cannot be assessed promptly, keep people away and avoid using or charging it. Smoke, fire or escalating heat calls for evacuation rather than waiting for a repair appointment. Keep children away from chargers and damaged packs. Include e-bikes and mobility equipment in the escape plan; a battery or vehicle must not block the only exit. swollen power bank battery swelling e bike battery lithium battery Check your equipment Use the specified compatible charger and reputable, certified equipment. Do not improvise repairs to a damaged pack. Choose a charging place Keep batteries away from combustible materials, direct sun and hot vehicles. Follow the product temperature limits. Notice changes early Stop using a device with unusual heat, changed shape, leaks, smells or sounds. Seek manufacturer or qualified repair advice rather than opening the pack. Dispose through the right service Do not put lithium batteries in household trash. Ask the local battery collection service how it handles damaged batteries before transporting one.

title: Long-duration blackout
summary: Plan around water, essential medical power, safe temperature, food and communications rather than a restoration estimate. Reserve battery power for necessities and use shelf-stable food when refrigeration fails. Keep all generators outdoors at least 20 feet from openings. Move early if essential care or safe shelter cannot be maintained.
text: Plan around water, essential medical power, safe temperature, food and communications rather than a restoration estimate. Reserve battery power for necessities and use shelf-stable food when refrigeration fails. Keep all generators outdoors at least 20 feet from openings. Move early if essential care or safe shelter cannot be maintained.  What runs out first? List the current water, food, medicine and battery supply in usable quantities. Compare these with actual household consumption. Check the next refill or relocation option while reserves still exist; counting unopened items is not enough when they need power or water to use. Which room should the household use? Choose the safest available room for temperature and accessible movement. Do not use a garage, fuel-burning appliance or a vehicle in an enclosed area for warmth or charging. Keep the exit and sanitation route clear. Shift from waiting to running a daily plan A long blackout becomes a problem of repeated decisions: drinking water, meals, sanitation, care, communication, rest, and movement. Treat the restoration estimate as uncertain. Build a plan that you can operate today, then review it as supplies and conditions change. This guide begins after the immediate hazards in the power-outage checklist have been addressed. A daily operating cycle Measure Count usable supplies and check people’s condition. Use actual quantities rather than how full a cupboard looks. Choose Decide the day’s meals, essential charging, check-ins, and whether home still meets important needs. Review Record what was used, what changed, and the trigger for the next action. Editorial planning cycle; urgent changes require action immediately, not at the next scheduled check. Use one notebook rather than scattered phone notes. Give each day a date and record the latest reliable information with its time. A handwritten log remains readable when batteries run out and helps a different adult take over without rebuilding the whole plan. Measure your runway with usable quantities Runway means the time a resource can support the household at the rate it is actually being used. Keep this as a planning estimate, not a promise. Do not count water of uncertain quality, food that cannot be safely prepared, or backup energy that cannot power the required device. A household status board you can copy into a notebook Need Write down Decision trigger Drinking water Safe amount available; actual daily use; next confirmed source Arrange supply or move before safe water is exhausted. Food Ready-to-eat meals suitable for everyone Change the meal plan before only unusable ingredients remain. Essential care Backup status; medicine storage; reachable support Act on the person-specific care deadline. Sanitation Handwashing water; waste route; toilet status Change arrangements if waste cannot be contained safely. Communication Working devices; charging opportunities; next check-in Use an agreed fallback if a channel fails. Transport Fuel or charge; driver; passable route; destination Preserve the ability to leave before options shrink. Example: 18 gallons of confirmed drinking-quality water divided by measured household use of 6 gallons a day suggests about three days of supply. It does not include uncounted guests, pets, spillage, or extra heat-related needs. Update the calculation after a day of real use. The goal is early decisions, never withholding necessary drinking water to make a number look better. Build a routine that reduces mistakes An example daily rhythm, adapted to your household When Useful tasks Morning Check people, water, food, sanitation, and current information. Decide whether to stay. Daylight Handle safe resupply, prepare the next meal, charge essentials when available, and check agreed contacts. Before dark Clear walking routes, place lights, organize night care, and confirm the next check-in. Evening Record use and problems. Protect a rest period for the adults responsible for care. Keep tasks small enough to complete. If one adult is caring for a child or dependent person, a complicated fuel schedule and multiple trips may be unrealistic. Build around the available help and physical ability. Use daylight for organizing, reading labels, and checking supplies, but avoid travel or exertion when weather or local conditions make those tasks unsafe. Give each recurring task an owner and an alternative person where possible. Use a check mark after a task is done; a discussion about doing it is not the same as completion. Keep children involved in age-appropriate tasks without giving them responsibility for fuel, hot equipment, electrical connections, or safety decisions. Preserve routines such as meals, medication schedules, and sleep as far as the individual care plan allows. Meals and hygiene without normal utilities Create a meal sequence from food that is already safe, familiar, and usable. Prefer portions the household can finish so you do not create leftovers that need refrigeration. Before opening a large container, work out how the remainder would be kept safe. A pantry of dry grains is not a complete plan if you lack safe cooking water or a permitted place to cook. Keep a manual opener with the meals that need it. Check soft-food needs, allergies, and food for pets. Separate safe drinking water from water reserved for an allowed non-drinking use. Clearly label containers so a tired person cannot confuse them. Choose a handwashing arrangement that can dispense safe water without repeated hand contact inside the supply container. If drainage or sewage may be affected, use the sanitation and sewer-failure guides rather than assuming that a toilet will keep working indefinitely. Waste management is part of the plan, not the last item to remember. Keep food waste away from meal preparation and sleeping areas, use appropriate containers, and check what collection or disposal route is actually available. Avoid instructions that depend on a nonexistent collection service or permit unsafe dumping. Emergency hygiene Sewer failure Food safety after power loss Protect care, communication, and rest Map the dependencies for each essential need. A powered device may also need a certain cable, clean water, consumables, an accessible outlet, or a trained caregiver. Write these together. A spare battery without the right adapter is not a working backup; a destination without accessibility may not meet the person’s actual needs. Make check-ins concise. State condition, location, immediate need, and next planned contact. Agree what a missed check-in means and what a supporter can safely do. Do not give every person a different schedule that becomes impossible to maintain. Preserve enough phone power for changes in condition and necessary movement. Use a real care threshold The point to seek another care setting comes from the person’s provider-approved plan and actual circumstances. Do not substitute a general household water or battery calculation for a clinical decision. Fatigue makes ordinary errors more likely: leaving a tap running, confusing containers, missing a care task, or stumbling over clutter. Arrange adult relief when available, keep the work area simple, and write down the important tasks. Someone living alone can ask a trusted contact for scheduled check-ins while still keeping a workable plan if contact fails. Resupply and relocation: make one complete decision Before a trip, decide what you need, where it is confirmed available, how to get there safely, and how to return. An unverified rumor about free ice can cost fuel, time, and phone charge. Combine necessary errands when appropriate, but do not turn a simple water trip into a long search while a vulnerable person is left unsupported. Questions to answer before leaving Question Why it matters Is the source open and the supply suitable? Avoid travelling to closed sites or accepting water of unclear quality. Can we carry the actual amount? Water, fuel, and equipment may exceed physical or vehicle capacity. Who stays with the household? Care, access, and essential monitoring still need to continue. What is the fallback? A failed trip should not leave no safe water or route to another location. Should this be a move rather than an errand? Repeated small trips may conceal that home no longer meets essential needs. If relocating, confirm the destination’s suitability, arrange transport, and take care information and essential equipment. Plan for pets and building access. If immediate danger develops, leave the hazard without delaying for a perfect inventory. Recovery and a useful after-action review After restoration, assess systems separately: electricity, drinking water, drainage, food storage, and communications. Do not assume one working service proves the others are ready. Use the relevant utility or public-health instructions, and qualified assessment for damaged equipment. Recharge and replenish the essentials that made the biggest difference. List the first shortage, the first equipment failure, and the hardest daily task. Identify a low-cost fix for each: a clearer label, a spare cable, a smaller water container, or a simpler meal. Update contact arrangements and relocation choices based on what was actually reachable. Review the plan with everyone who will use it, including a substitute caregiver. A useful review ends with a short list of changes you can make, not a wish list of expensive equipment. Keep the plan modest enough that you will maintain it between emergencies. Share safe tasks and checked information with trusted neighbours. Charge essential devices when safe power is available and use brief scheduled check-ins. Do not rely on an internet-only plan. An announced restoration time is an estimate. Carbon monoxide, unsafe improvised wiring, dehydration and dangerous temperatures can be more urgent than the outage itself. Build a daily plan from current supplies and reachable shelter options. Do not wait for a food distribution, public generator or rescue transport that has not been confirmed. Plan shifts for checking vulnerable people and essential equipment so one caregiver is not awake continuously. Keep infant feeding, safe sleep, medicine storage and pet water on the same written daily inventory. extended blackout days without power grid down prolonged power outage Shift from waiting to running a daily plan Measure your runway with usable quantities Build a routine that reduces mistakes Meals and hygiene without normal utilities Protect care, communication, and rest Resupply and relocation: make one complete decision Recovery and a useful after-action review List critical needs Identify power-dependent care, temperature-sensitive medicines, water access and who cannot manage stairs or heat. Set priorities before using scarce batteries or fuel. Measure what remains Write down safe water, ready-to-eat meals, usable batteries and medicine quantities. Review the inventory daily rather than guessing. Keep fuel use safe Never run generators, charcoal or camping stoves indoors, in a garage or on an enclosed balcony. Do not backfeed house wiring. Protect food and hygiene Keep cold appliances closed and use food-safety time and temperature guidance. Separate drinking water from washing and waste arrangements. Set a relocation trigger Choose the point when medical support, water or temperature can no longer be maintained. Confirm a reachable destination before those needs become urgent.

title: Lost outdoors
summary: Stop moving, stay together and assess your last known position. If there is no immediate threat, stay put, protect yourself from weather and signal for help. Share your location if communication works; do not wander in search of a shortcut.
text: No signal Prepare a short location message, reduce battery use and use visible or audible signals. Do not wander solely to make the phone work. Immediate threat at the waiting place Relocate the shortest practical distance to lower danger and record the new location. Staying put is conditional on the site being safe. Should someone go for help? Splitting up can create additional lost people. Use communication or a trusted passing person where possible; avoid an unplanned solo search for a road. Avoid making the search area larger Stop at a safe position, assess immediate hazards and use your last reliable map location. Stay put when lost unless the location itself is unsafe. Unplanned downhill travel, river following or shortcuts can introduce cliffs, floodwater and greater distance from your itinerary. Make a precise help message Report location or the last confirmed landmark, group size, injuries, weather exposure and available supplies. State if you must move for immediate safety. Use safe visible signaling and your trip contact’s overdue plan; do not exhaust yourself repeatedly shouting or searching for a phone signal. Give rescuers coordinates, last known location, group size, injuries and equipment. When a location is shared, stay there unless a direct threat forces a move. A phone compass or GPS reading is not a safe route by itself. Do not climb hazardous ridges for a signal or enter moving water. Use the supplies and shelter you already have; do not assume a rescue is underway until communication confirms it. Leave a clear note of time, direction and destination only if immediate danger forces a move. Avoid dividing the party or attempting unverified routes in darkness. Keep children and less mobile companions beside an adult. Check everyone for cold, heat and exhaustion and inventory each person’s supplies. Before a trip, leave a route, return time and overdue plan with a trusted contact.  Stop and assess Check injury, weather, daylight and remaining supplies. Mark your location and the last reliable landmark on an offline map if available. Choose a safe waiting place Move only enough to escape immediate hazards such as floodwater, falling trees or exposed severe weather. Keep the group together and tell contacts if your location changes. Protect from exposure Use available layers and shelter to reduce wet, wind, cold or sun exposure. Avoid hazardous terrain while trying to improve a shelter. Signal and conserve Use a whistle, bright material or light when appropriate. Call or send a location message if possible; conserve phone power between attempts.

title: Map and compass: a practical navigation foundation
summary: Learn your map, compass and route before going somewhere unfamiliar. Carry a physical map alongside electronic navigation and a way to keep the phone powered. A compass indicates direction; it cannot tell you whether terrain is passable or whether you are on the correct trail.
text: You cannot identify your position? Stop and reassess rather than inventing a route. The planned terrain is unsafe? Use the turnaround or alternate plan. Will a compass work without mobile reception? A conventional magnetic compass does not need reception, but you still need the right map, a known position and the skills to interpret them. A simple route card Editorial fields: start, intended route, obvious junctions, turnaround point, expected return and alternate exit. Use landmarks you can recognize on the ground. Keep the first practice route short and familiar so a mistaken turn is easy to notice and correct. A compass is one part of the decision Practice with qualified instruction for bearings, map orientation and local magnetic declination before relying on those techniques. Do not choose a straight-line shortcut merely because the compass points that way. Rivers, cliffs, private land and weather can make a direction unusable. Practice a failed-phone scenario On a familiar safe route, compare the physical map with known junctions while keeping the phone available for real emergencies. Can everyone identify the start, return route and turnaround point? Stop the exercise if you become unsure of your position. Choose a safe introductory navigation session and a short familiar practice walk. Expand only when you can explain your route and backup without relying on one screen. Electronic location can be inaccurate or unavailable. A bearing does not establish a safe crossing, legal access or a clear path through unfamiliar terrain. When navigation becomes uncertain, stop making the situation worse. Reassess your known location, daylight, weather and group needs. Use the lost-outdoors guide rather than walking on a guess. Match distance, pace and turnaround time to the slowest group member.
